articles.title: More art, less artificial: Seattle Art Museum billboards troll tech ads and tell people to look up
articles.author: Kurt Schlosser
paras: A billboard taking a swipe at Anthropic’s Claude might sound like the work of a rival AI company. This one is from the Seattle Art Museum .

“The only Claude you need is Monet,” the sign reads. It’s part of the latest wave of messages in SAM’s “Dear Seattle” campaign, which has spent the fall urging people to look up from their screens and see something in person.

Earlier billboards around the city told passersby to “come stare at something that isn’t your inbox” and noted that “even the algorithm thinks you should get out more.” The final batch pushes the AI jokes further, including one asking for “a little more art and a little less artificial” and another promising, “Your phone doesn’t have to know.”
Tech billboards are a fixture in the San Francisco Bay Area, where AI startups cover Highway 101 and city streets with ads that often mean little to anyone outside the industry.

They’re less common around Seattle. Anthropic put up a big orange Claude billboard over Aurora Avenue in 2024, and this spring Bellevue startup Summation put one up along SR 520 because “startup energy should be more visible around here,” its CEO told GeekWire.

“In a city where so much of our lives happens on screens, we’re making a playful case for the things you can only experience in person,” Kat Bryant Flaherty, SAM’s director of communications, said in a statement. She listed “the scale and texture of an artwork, a film with a room full of strangers, making something with your hands, or catching up with a friend over a meal.”

The campaign is tied to changes at the downtown museum itself, where SAM is adding more public space and more reasons to linger, including hands-on art making and music in the Studio at SAM and the newly opened Bar Dojo restaurant.
The campaign runs through the end of the year, with more than 200 ads across the region — more than 20 billboards plus spots on light rail and digital kiosks.
SAM’s campaign is about the same size as the one Bellevue startup Statsig ran in the Bay Area in 2024, with more than 200 billboards and transit posters, but pointed in the opposite direction.

SAM is offering buy-one-get-one-free tickets in December with the code “LOVESAM,” good at both the downtown museum and the Seattle Asian Art Museum in Volunteer Park, to encourage people to visit together.
“We’re hoping to grab attention, spark curiosity, and remind Seattle that there’s a lot happening at SAM worth leaving the house for,” Flaherty said.

articles.title: Living Computers closed, but its spirit and vintage machines live on at a museum south of Seattle
articles.author: Kurt Schlosser
paras: When Seattle’s Living Computers: Museum + Labs closed for good in 2024, it seemed like the end of the line for anyone who wanted to do more than just look at old computers.
But in a Tukwila business park 20 minutes south of downtown, a sizable collection of vintage computers is still alive — kept running by a few of the same people who once did the same for Paul Allen.

The Interim Computer Museum is a nonprofit that opened to the public in 2024 and has quietly grown into a hands-on showcase of dozens of machines, from early Apples and IBM PCs to hulking DEC systems that once filled university labs. At 4,400 square feet of public space, it’s nearly as big as Living Computers was before that museum expanded in 2016.

ICM is led by Stephen Jones , who calls himself the museum’s “caretaker.” Jones spent two decades helping track down and restore machines for Allen, first at PDP Planet, Allen’s private collection of vintage systems, then at Living Computers, where he was senior engineering manager.

When the late Microsoft co-founder’s estate wound down Living Computers, the majority of the collection went to the Mimms Museum of Technology and Art in Georgia , where Jones is also a curator. The machines in Tukwila are privately owned, and Jones has helped bankroll ICM with personal funds, with plans to eventually donate the collection to the nonprofit.
He chose not to reuse the Living Computers name, which ICM now holds, because “it has a finite past.” Instead, he wants to carry on “the spirit of the engineering focus.”
“Between Mimms and here, this is the legacy,” Jones said. “We show the name and the connection to the past, but we’re doing new things.”

ICM occupies space in Seattle Exchange @ Southcenter , a sprawl of low-slung flex buildings off Strander Boulevard near Westfield Southcenter mall. Its neighbors include a car detailer, a pest control company, a welding shop, an embroiderer and an upholsterer.

More than four decades ago, Seattle Computer Products operated just down Industry Drive. That’s where Tim Paterson wrote 86-DOS, the operating system Microsoft bought and turned into MS-DOS for IBM’s first PC.

Jones calls that proximity part of the “magic” of the location. The museum has a Gazelle computer that SCP built nearby, using boards that Jones said the company hired high school students to assemble and test. Volunteers recently pulled data off its hard drive, which boots into MS-DOS 2.11 and still holds SCP’s own source code.

Allen’s fingerprints are everywhere. One display holds a 1971 letter from Hellmut Golde, director of the University of Washington’s Computer Science Laboratory, kicking Allen and his “friends from the Lakeside School” out of the lab. Among the offenses: tying up the teletypes to print “endless listings,” and taking an acoustic coupler from a professor’s office “without leaving at least a note.” Golde asked them to turn in their keys.

The letter sits beside an Imlac PDS-1, the same type of graphics computer Golde scolded the teens for using without permission. More than five decades later, the letter is headed back to campus: ICM plans to display it, along with the Imlac, at UW’s 60th anniversary celebration for its computer science program in March.

Jones recalled that Allen insisted visitors to Living Computers get “the 10-minute experience” of loading an Altair 8800 from paper tape, just as he remembered it. The kit computer was the machine for which Allen and Bill Gates wrote Microsoft’s first product, and Allen wanted to reinforce “how far we’ve come and how difficult old computers were.” ICM has an Altair 8800 on display .

Around the corner is Miss Piggy, a DEC datasystem 570 that Microsoft used in the early 1980s to support the group that built Multiplan, Word and later Excel. It was also the email host for much of the company, including Gates, who once had to print out an important message on its console printer when the system went down before a speaking engagement.

Recovered email shows Allen pushing to get Piggy networked. “Paul Allen is very keen on doing this,” Henry Burgess wrote in 1982. Retired in 1986, the machine now runs again in Tukwila. It’s one of ICM’s most popular remote systems, and some fans come in just to write programs while sitting next to it.

Other local ties include a PDP-7 that Boeing used to process flight data in the 1960s, and a Toad-1, a modern take on the PDP-10 built in the 1990s by Redmond’s XKL. Jones first got involved with Allen’s world through a 1997 Usenet post inviting PDP-10 enthusiasts onto a Toad. That machine became the cornerstone of PDP Planet.
In a 2024 video for Christie’s , Jones said what inspired Allen was “being able to recover old programs, mythical code, and get them running on hardware so that they can be studied.”
Asked what Allen would make of ICM, Jones didn’t hesitate. “I think he’d be happy,” he said.
On a monitor beside ICM’s PDP-6, a 1968 artificial intelligence program is having trouble.
“SORRY, I DON’T KNOW THE WORD ‘STEEPLE,'” it replies.

The program is SHRDLU, created by Terry Winograd at the MIT AI Lab. It let a user type plain-English commands to move blocks around a virtual world. Only the PDP-6’s front console and display survived, so ICM is rebuilding the machine as a “hybrid,” with the original hardware wired to an emulator.

Jones sees a lesson in that old error message. “You look at this and you think of how we use ChatGPT now,” he said. “The cool thing about SHRDLU is that it can tell you ‘I don’t know.’ It doesn’t try to fabricate anything.”

ICM has its own ties to the modern AI world. An Anthropic employee is a member and strong supporter, and in October the museum brought six vintage computing stations to an Anthropic event, where the company’s Claude chatbot wrote programs for machines like the Commodore 64.

Back in Tukwila, Claude has become one of ICM’s most useful restoration tools. The team feeds it huge stacks of scanned documentation, such as the full set of schematics for a PDP-10. When a machine has a logic fault, they ask where to look, and Claude points them to a page in the maintenance manual or a likely bad module.
“That’s turned things that would take a couple of weeks to solve into a couple of days,” Jones said.

AI can point the way, but the repairs remain hands-on work. When Miss Piggy wouldn’t run properly this year, former Living Computers engineer Josh Dersch stepped through the machine’s microcode one instruction at a time using a recreated DEC test board, until he found a single bad chip. A spare board brought it back.

Asked if it still takes a human to keep these machines running, Jones agreed — at least for now. If a humanoid robot with AI built in ever shows up to do the repairs, he joked, “then I sit at the front desk all day.”

Nearly everything at ICM is meant to be touched, switched on and played with, and that can be intimidating. On machines with nothing but a text prompt, “you kind of have to know the commands in your head already,” Jones said.

That’s by design. From the start, the idea was to challenge people “either by confronting them with their past or demonstrating how difficult it was,” Jones said. His example: two friends, one with an Apple IIe and one with an IBM PC, whose computers “could never share” software. ICM continues that legacy, he said, “challenging the visitor to go beyond what they might feel comfortable with.”

Volunteers have written cheat sheets to help newcomers, and Jones is encouraged when families come in and kids start typing BASIC programs. “That to me was the spirit of what PDP Planet and Living Computers was meant to be,” he said.

Very little is behind glass. Jones jokes that a Timex Sinclair 1000, which would wipe your painstakingly typed program if you bumped it, is “the only computer that deserves to be behind glass.” The goal, he said, is to avoid “a boneyard that people walk through.”

Other highlights include Galaxy Game , the first coin-operated video game, installed at Stanford in 1971 and now being restored, and a Thinking Machines CM-2 supercomputer, whose 40th anniversary ICM just celebrated with members of its original design team.

For younger engineers raised on modern tools, Jones has a go-to move. He asks if they’ve used Linux, then walks them over to the PDP-7, the type of machine Unix was first written on more than 50 years ago. Many of the basic commands they type every day started there.

The collection totals about 6,000 artifacts. Volunteers are also slowly working through roughly 3,000 magnetic tapes and disk packs from Living Computers’ software preservation program. And ICM keeps 32 historic systems online, where members can log in from anywhere to use vintage operating systems, programming languages and games.

That remote access helps explain why ICM has about 500 members and sponsors, even though only 81 members have visited in person this year. Memberships start at $36 a year. Along with a King County grant through 4Culture, they help cover rent, with personal funds from Jones filling the gap. The museum hopes to become self-sustaining within five years, and maybe someday buy its own building.

The museum’s name reflects the urgency. “We’re in this magic window right now, where the hardware can still run, we can still maintain it, you can replace parts,” Jones said. “But slowly we’re getting further and further away.”

ICM is open Saturdays through Mondays from 10 a.m. to 4 p.m. Admission is $9 for adults and free for those under 18. Last May, the museum revived Vintage Computer Festival Pacific Northwest, which had been canceled in March 2020. The event drew 981 people, and it returns May 1–2 at the Tukwila Community Center.

Among the machines on the floor is MIT-AI, a DECsystem-2020 that once served as the ARPANET host for MIT’s Artificial Intelligence Lab. As Living Computers shut down in 2024, Christopher Zach, who sold the machine to Allen, told GeekWire he was ready to drive a U-Haul to Seattle to rescue it.
When a friend of Zach’s stopped by ICM’s booth at WorldCon and asked about “Chris’s computer,” Jones had a simple message to pass along: “Please just tell him it’s safe.”

articles.title: Electric boat maker Zin Boats raises $5M and launches propulsion business beyond the water
articles.author: Kurt Schlosser
paras: Zin Boats made a splash with fast, pricey electric boats. But most of its business is now coming from what’s under the floor.

The Seattle startup has launched Zin Power , a new division that will supply its electric propulsion systems to other boat builders and to industries that rely on diesel engines, such as construction and mining.
The company also raised $5 million to scale up production and expanded its headquarters in the Interbay neighborhood to 11,000 square feet.

About 90% of the company’s revenue comes from selling motors and batteries to customers in the marine and drone industries, founder and CEO Piotr Zin told GeekWire. A typical setup includes two motors and about 500 kilowatt-hours of battery storage.
“We noticed a steady demand for pleasure craft year over year, but at the same time a massive increase in propulsion sales,” Zin said.
Customers include StanCraft Wooden Boats, which teamed with Zin on the 340 Hammerhead E, an all-electric wooden runabout. StanCraft delivered the first one to a customer this summer.

GeekWire first checked out the company in early 2024, when it was relaunching after a pandemic shutdown with its Z2R , a 20-foot carbon fiber runabout. Later that year Zin showed off the Z11, a 37-foot electric tender designed to shuttle passengers to and from megayachts at more than 60 mph. The company said boats on the platform would cost $1.75 million to $3.75 million.

The company also offers the Z7 Convertible , a 22-foot runabout with a removable roof that it pitches for fishing, surfing and cruising. The boat has a top speed of 40 mph and a range of more than 80 miles

Zin Power grew out of the drivetrains engineered for those boats. Zin sees the marine track record as a selling point for other industries that need high torque, including construction, mining and remotely operated vehicles (ROVs).
“The ocean is one of the harshest environments there is, so the technology has already proven itself under about the toughest conditions it could face,” Zin said.
Many of those machines still run on diesel engines, a technology more than a century old. Zin said operators are eager to switch to electric.
“What’s interesting is that economics is driving the shift, not regulation or image,” he said.

Electric systems cost up to 70% less to operate, according to Zin. He estimated that replacing a single 250-horsepower industrial diesel engine that runs eight hours a day could save as much as $1.5 million over 10 years.

The new funding will pay for more manufacturing capacity, a dedicated sales and engineering team to work with boat builders, and support for customers converting from diesel. Zin calls it a seed round, with a larger raise planned down the road. The company has raised $6.5 million to date, including a $1.275 million seed round in early 2024.
Zin Boats has nine full-time employees and brings on about a dozen contractors as needed.

For now, each Zin Power system is built to order. The company’s motors range from 100 to 600 kilowatts and deliver up to 2,700 pound-feet of torque, and its systems can run fully electric or as hybrids. A proprietary control unit that Zin Power calls the “Magic Box” manages everything from charging and cooling to software and safety.

“Our goal is to keep delivering what we’ve built while developing simpler, more advanced plug-and-play systems,” Zin said. “Eventually, we want a customer to be able to pull out a diesel engine and drop in a Zin Power system as a direct one-for-one replacement.”

articles.title: Uncommon Thinkers: Saf Rabah wants to make it easier to build housing, one permit at a time
articles.author: Grace Kaste
paras: Editor’s note: This series profiles five Seattle-area “Uncommon Thinkers,” who will be recognized Dec. 10 at the GeekWire Gala in partnership with Greater Seattle Partners .

When startup founder Safouen (Saf) Rabah decided to get in on the AI boom, he didn’t start by coding or by training any models. He got in touch with urban planners at Bellevue City Hall, and together they combed through nearly 300 land use permit applications to find common mistakes and bottlenecks.

Bellevue began using Rabah’s platform, Govstream.AI , in the summer of 2025, starting with an AI assistant for city staff. In a test using past applications, about three times as many were judged complete with Govstream’s tool. Rabah says that change alone has the potential to alter the housing stock of the city.

“Why can’t we build more housing? All the macro economic reasons, inflation, material costs, labor, land scarcity, are all exacerbated by the slow permitting process,” Rabah said. “That’s what we want to change.”
So, how did Rabah, a B2B software engineer by training, find his way to land use permitting?

Rabah hadn’t heard of the government technology sector, aka GovTech, until mid-career, but looking back, the signs were all there. He was born in Sfax, Tunisia, and grew up in Tunis. Throughout his childhood, he dreamed of running for office.

“I come from a small developing country, so there’s always this idea of, what could a small developing country become? How can it prosper and grow?” Rabah said. “Building has always been a big part of what I imagined myself doing.”

As a teenager in the 1980s, he attended a USAID-funded boarding school in Tunis. The school was part of Cold War efforts to expand American soft power around the Middle East; classes were conducted in English and many of the students went on to university in North America.
“The school had the first Macintosh lab in all of Africa,” Rabah said. “I can still picture the USAID logo on the back of each computer.”

Rabah got a scholarship to University of British Columbia, where he studied electrical engineering while running what he calls his “first entrepreneurial venture”: a service that built and hosted websites for small businesses.

That led to a job at a startup called Pivotal, a customer relationship management platform where Rabah led a team responsible for e-business applications. After Pivotal went public, Rabah left for a job at TELUS, one of Canada’s “big three” telecommunications corporations, but quickly felt frustrated by the dynamics at such a large company.
“Even though I worked on nascent products, it was very, very bureaucratic,” Rabah said. “There were committees, a hundred thousand employees. I missed building things.”
Rabah began to look for a new job that would not only allow him to build but also to make a difference.

“Being an immigrant, it’s always tempting to stay content with having a good job, good status,” Rabah said. “But I’ve always enjoyed the ‘what if?’ mindset, the clean slate. It’s this way today, but could we imagine it to be something different?”
That vision led him to Socrata, which in 2010 was just a nascent government technology startup.
“I really connected with the founder,” Rabah said. “It had a really cool mission, it combined the ‘do-well’ with ‘do-good.’”

Socrata was one of the first platforms to host data portals for local governments and federal agencies, allowing citizens to access and map public data sets. Many U.S. cities, including Seattle, still use Socrata’s software today to publish information including crime logs, permits, and budgets.
“We were a big part of pioneering the open data movement,” Rabah said. “At one point almost every major city was our customer, and half the states.”
Socrata was acquired by Tyler Technologies in 2018, and Rabah stayed on until 2024.

“The funny part is today we use that data quite a lot in our work because one of the most popular data sets that any city publishes is its permit data,” Rabah said. “We’ve even built a connector between Socrata and Govstream.”
But once Socrata was acquired, Rabah began to feel the same way he had at TELUS: boxed in by bureaucracy.
“Tyler was a really good company, but it is a big company,” Rabah said. “Tech was getting repetitive, and I was thinking about leaving it altogether.”

“The thing that pushed me over the edge is that AI happened,” Rabah said. “It was one of those moments where once you start working with it, you really can’t help but think, ‘I can revisit virtually every assumption I’ve made over the last 20 years, every constraint.’”
Immediately, he thought of his passion for building—building a startup, building a better country, and literally building a building.

“I’ve been fascinated by the built environment since my Lego days: What makes some cities livable and others not?” Rabah said. “Then, living in Seattle, you see the lack of housing, affordability, and the homelessness problem we have, and you’re like, why can’t we build more housing? I started believing that these problems are in fact solvable if we simply speed things up and simplify things with AI.”
In July of 2024, Rabah began working with his “design partner,” Bellevue’s Development Services Department, to learn more about common permitting problems.

“We started with something visionary and high-level, but you can only get there if you understand the granular problems of the day-to-day,” Rabah said. “So we talked with developers and builders and we talked with the people on the other side of the counter who are processing these permits and guiding these builders.”

He learned that most permitting mistakes are avoidable, like applying for the wrong zone or forgetting to include a north arrow on an architectural plan. Those oversights can send an application back to square one while clogging up the permitting process for all other projects.
“The wait time disproportionately affects lower margin projects,” Rabah said. “It really constrains the supply of housing, especially the housing we need more of, which is the more affordable kind.”

Govstream’s AI assistants are designed to help first-time builders avoid those errors and make permitting faster for everyone. Rabah and his team began by building what they call an “intelligent intake” platform for a city permitting portal, which guided users through preparing to submit their applications.

When Bellevue first tested Govstream’s intake tool on 276 past residential building permit applications, the city reported a completeness rate of 67%, compared with 22% when those applications were originally filed. According to the company, the latest testing has yielded an 88% completeness rate.

More recently, they’ve begun to build out an AI assistant for the backend, which assists city permit techs with the initial review and reduces what Rabah calls “toil,” like answering unnecessary pre-application emails and tracking down missing documents.
Bellevue staff estimated that Govstream’s tools saved them 152 hours over one month this summer by helping them research and respond to pre-application inquiries.

“For a developer, time is money, so the type of housing that can be built in Bellevue will become more affordable,” said Jake Hesselgesser, Bellevue’s development services director. “This technology has a direct and material impact on the cost of housing.”
Eventually, Govstream.AI will be an end-to-end service, assisting in later stages of the permitting process, too. But Rabah is emphatic that Govstream will not give AI the final say.
“We always put our AI systems in the role of assistants that suggest stuff, but never decide stuff,” Rabah said.

Rabah says Govstream uses preset rules, outside the AI model, to check whether a portion of the application is complete, whether a site needs a geotechnical report, or whether an architect is properly licensed. In Bellevue, city staff retain final authority.
Hesselgesser said that Rabah’s conservative approach to AI is what made the city of Bellevue want to work with his startup.

“Our core principle around Bellevue’s use of AI is to retain human decision making, and we wanted to ensure that we were aligned with a company with the same core value,” Hesselgesser said. “Saf took that holistic approach.”

Around the office, Rabah has become known for his eagerness to build. According to Mariia Derevianko, head of marketing, he spends his weekends building out a product or an idea in order to workshop it with the team.

articles.title: SenseNet lands $43M financing deal for early wildfire detection and intelligence
articles.author: Lisa Stiffler
paras: SenseNet , a startup providing wildfire detection and intelligence, on Tuesday announced a $43 million financing package. The Vancouver, B.C.-based company says the funding will support its expansion across the U.S. and internationally.

The startup uses a suite of technologies for the rapid detection of wildfires, including environmental sensors, AI-enabled cameras, satellite data, drone technology and predictive analytics. Its monitoring footprint covers 450 million acres in a dozen countries.
SenseNet says its technology has provided early alerts for more than 10,000 fires, in some cases hours before the first 911 calls.

“Wildfire protection is no longer just about detecting a fire as quickly as possible. It’s about understanding what’s happening, what could happen next, and giving the right people the information they need to act,” Hamed Noori , co-founder and CEO of SenseNet, said in a statement.
Noori launched SenseNet in 2019 with Chief Technology Officer Shahab Bahrami . Both hold doctorates in electrical and computer engineering from the University of British Columbia.
The Series B round was led by Idealist Capital , with participation from Fusion Fund , Stormbreaker Ventures , Thin Line Capital , National Bank of Canada and The Sitka Foundation .

The financing includes purchases of newly issued shares, which put money into SenseNet; secondary share sales, which pay existing shareholders; and debt. SenseNet did not disclose how much of the $43 million falls into each category.
The startup previously raised $12.78 million and has 30 employees, according to PitchBook.

SenseNet competes with companies including OroraTech, Dryad and Pano AI, whose cameras, software and alerting services are used by Washington’s Department of Natural Resources to detect wildfires. The companies are developing their technology as warming temperatures and drier conditions increase wildfire risks.

articles.title: Copilot without M365, and more news you didn’t hear (but maybe should have) at Microsoft Ignite
articles.author: Mary Jo Foley
paras: Many Microsoft business customers are still wading through the session slide decks and “Book of News” collection of product and strategy announcements from Microsoft’s Ignite confab last week. But not all the new goodies announced there (or simultaneous with this year’s Microsoft Ignite show , which kicked off Nov. 17) might have made it onto everyone’s radar.

Microsoft’s curated Ignite keynote and session spotlights were, unsurprisingly, dedicated to Microsoft AI in all its guises — Copilot, the Microsoft IQ intelligence platforms and Agent 365. But there was some other important news last week that Microsoft customers could find equally, if not more, interesting and useful.
Among my picks for the “make sure you didn’t miss this” list:

Copilot without the M365 subscription prerequisite arrives next week : Despite a LOT of talk about Copilot, “a new OS for work,” Microsoft didn’t mention anything at all during Ignite about a new purchasing option for Copilot that is set to go live on Dec. 1. Starting then, Microsoft will offer a version of Copilot to small business and enterprise customers without the current prerequisite of having a certain paid Microsoft 365 plan.

For a flat fee of $21 per user per month for small businesses and $30 per user per month for enterprise customers (before discounts), users will be able to buy this new standalone Copilot offering, as Microsoft quietly announced back in October on its Partner Center site.

Currently, to buy Copilot, business customers need to have purchased a qualifying Microsoft 365 subscription plan before they shell out even more money for Copilot. Because of this requirement, Microsoft isn’t competitive price-wise when pitted against OpenAI’s ChatGPT or Anthropic’s Claude entry-level business tiers.
The new offer is for new customers buying through any of Microsoft’s channels, including its Cloud Solution Provider program, across commercial, education, government and nonprofit sectors.

I’ve got a lot of questions about this new offer, including where Copilot chats are stored and how/if customers will get some kind of access to the Microsoft IQ technology that underlies Copilot and is positioned as its secret sauce if they don’t have a Microsoft 365 subscription. I’ve asked Microsoft, but no word back so far.

Azure Linux 4.0 is now ready for prime time : Announced on the same day Ignite kicked off (but without a mention during the conference), Microsoft’s own commercial Linux distribution, Azure Linux 4.0, is now generally available .

The 4.0 release is interesting for a few reasons. First, it is the first release of Azure Linux — formerly known as Common Base Linux (CBL)-Mariner — designed as a general-purpose server OS for customer virtual machines, and it is based on the Fedora Linux stack. Checking off the requisite AI box, Azure Linux 4.0 is “purpose-built for cloud native and AI workloads,” as Microsoft said back in May.

Microsoft officials have said two-thirds of customer cores in Azure run Linux (not Windows Server). Microsoft has acknowledged the platforms running Microsoft 365, GitHub and OpenAI’s ChatGPT “all sit on Linux foundations.”
Microsoft has supported a wide variety of Linux distributions on Azure for years but never made its own available for commercial use by customers and partners until now.

Windows Server 2028 is in the works : Yes, another on-premises version of Windows Server is coming. Christened Windows Server 2028 , the next release, likely to debut in late 2027, is now in public preview.
Microsoft mentioned Server 2028 in its Book of News and in passing in some sessions, but it was not positioned as a top-tier announcement.

The 2028 release includes some expected and a few surprise features, such as making 32-bit app support an optional component rather than installing it by default. That change, along with a hardened Server Core configuration included by default, is designed to improve the security of the platform from the get-go. But they may present potential backward-compatibility risks .

Microsoft is positioning Server 2028 similarly to the way it has been pushing Windows client lately: as a way to run AI workloads more cheaply because they can run locally. The “unmetered intelligence” pitch strikes again.
Sure, Microsoft can’t make every announcement a centerpiece in a two-plus-hour (waah!) opening keynote. But sometimes, hidden gems deserve their moments in the sun. Or pouring rain …

articles.title: Delridge Station bus loop
articles.author: Martin Pagel
paras: Earlier this year Sound Transit provided a simplified design for the Delridge Link Station. If the West Seattle Link Extension gets built, Ross pointed out how RapidRide H buses will need to detour to serve the station. That would eliminate any travel time advantages gained by running on rails even if bus and trains would align their departure time perfectly. Instead of such detour, what about if the buses would just stop on Delridge Way and riders could take an overpass to the platform going north? It’s similar to RapidRide A buses stopping on International Blvd and riders taking an overpass to reach the airport station.
As most riders are expected to reach the station by bus, in particular RapidRide H, the transfer experience will be critical.

Early on Sound Transit had considered various designs for the Delridge Link station. Before settling on the location in front of the steel plant, one such design had been right above and along Delridge Way. Busses would have stopped right underneath, and riders could have just taken an escalator up to the departing platform. That would have provided a great transfer experience. With the current alignment and station location, designing a great transfer experience is more complicated. For southbound buses, Sound Transit plans a station along Delridge Way. For northbound buses, Sound Transit proposes that the buses detour from the red bus lane on the right to take a left turn into SW Andover St and a right turn into the station (see blue line on map below). But that also means buses have to pull out of the station and turn left again to get back to Delridge Way. Along the way they may need to navigate around the large trucks serving the steel plant. While riders get dropped off right under the Link platform, the various turns each bus has to navigate may add several minutes to the transfer.

If Sound Transit would instead add a northbound bus stop along Delridge Way across from the southbound bus stop and an overpass connecting to the northbound Link platform (see red lines on map), then riders could arrive quite quickly. (Southbound riders would need to take the escalator/elevator down and up again)

Sound Transit already plans a staircase on the NE corner of the station. Instead, they could build a staircase on the east side of Delridge Way and connect it with an overpass to the northbound platform. This would be similar to the way buses stop along the International Blvd to reach the airport station.

This would free up bus bays on the west side of the station. That space could be used as pickup/drop off and paratransit stop which may eliminate the need for the south car/van loop. That may allow larger housing developments on the south corner.

I am also concerned that the station entrance is quite a bit lower than Delridge Way. That may create some issues for riders who want to walk on the ground between buses along Delridge and the station. I really liked the plaza of the prior station design which allowed access to a mezzanine but understand that it adds cost. It would be great if the housing development could connect at least to the south staircases and elevators midway. If Sound Transit could add a small mezzanine under the tracks connecting the northbound and southbound southern staircases, it would help with at-grade walking to Delridge (and also switching platforms).

I still don’t think a Link extension to West Seattle is a good choice as buses could just drop riders off at SODO, but if we proceed with the plan, let’s at least optimize the existing design to improve the transfer experience as much as possible.

articles.title: Sound Transit Inches Forward Station Activation and Retail Plan
articles.author: Doug Trumm
paras: In leading transit systems around the world, shops and cafes are often integrated into the fabric of stations, with busier hubs even melding into full-scale shopping malls. That's decidedly not the case for the retail-scarce Sound Transit network or for most other agencies across the Seattle metropolitan area.

However, as Sound Transit has grown into the busiest light rail system in the United States, boasting more than 160,000 daily riders, policymakers are beginning to ask if it's time to change that. Sound Transit has implemented a few pilot programs, but a broader activation strategy could be on the horizon, potentially building out retail and community programming on a larger scale.

"Much of the work is still in early testing and pilot stages, but we are refining proof of concepts, and we do have an eye for wider expansions," Marie Olson, Sound Transit's executive director of rider experience and operations, told agency board members during a November 5 meeting.

Most of Sound Transit's early efforts at retail installations are located outside of Seattle, although Seattle (which is home to a majority of the region's light rail ridership ) has seen a few temporary markets and festivals near its stations, as have some suburban stations.

Early efforts at creating permanent retail at Seattle stations have failed to take root. One enterprising vendor pushed to open up a coffee cart at Capitol Hill Station, but ran into health code hurdles and general bureaucratic morass that forced them to close up shop, as The Urbanist reported in June. Capitol Hill remains one of Sound Transit busiest stations, so the opportunity remains once startup hurdles are cleared.

In 2022, Sound Transit welcomed a coffee shop before the neighboring Redmond Technology Station had even opened to light rail riders. At a presentation to the Rider Experience and Operations (REO) Committee on November 5, Marshall Foster, chief planning and development officer for Sound Transit, christened the project a success, pointing out that the Microsoft campus provides a built-in audience for the Dote coffee bar.

"Another interesting example is the Redmond Technology Station, where we have the Microsoft Coffee Bar," Foster said. "That's your more traditional, built-out brick-and-mortar retail space. I think we learned there that the power of having a built-in daily audience and market for retail is critical."

While Microsoft's Redmond HQ campus touts a headcount above 50,000, the light rail station next door is posting more modest figures, with just over 1,000 daily boardings. That's about a quarter of the boardings typically seen at a median 1 Line station, suggesting ample retail opportunities across the system. The modest ridership so far also hints that a good chunk of customers are visiting the coffee bar without riding light rail before or after.

In 2023, the agency opened The Roadhouse in Angle Lake, serving as a community performance space. That endeavor followed a failed attempt at retail at the site, illustrating that issues with creating nearby storefronts aren't always on Sound Transit's end.
In 2025, a coffee shop opened at Lynnwood Station, and a hotdog stand recently set up shop at Federal Way.

"At Lynnwood City Center Station, we had a vacant space, which was purpose-built for a cafe-style vending, and we worked closely with Lynnwood and Snohomish Chambers [of Commerce]," Olson said. "We spread the word out to get solicitations. We also worked with the city of Lynnwood to get that word out. Caffe Ciao is in there now. They opened in the summer of 2025. Today they operate seven days a week, Monday through Friday, 5 am to 5 pm and Saturday and Sunday, 8 am to 3 pm. And they just renewed their lease for another two years."
Olson noted that Federal Way's hot dog stand is on a seven-month trial run.

"Our newest vendor [...] is Whatzz Up Dogg," Olson said. "[It] just opened this summer at Federal Way Downtown Station Plaza, and it's got a seven-month trial. It's a great spot, and it really brings that station to life if you've been out there."

Tacoma Councilmember Kristina Walker, who chairs the REO committee, agreed, saying the hot dog vendor "is the nicest, friendliest, most welcoming person ever, and he really has changed the energy at that station, I love it. So more of that. He's doing a great job."
Systemwide, riders have expressed strong interest in station retail, according to agency surveys.
"We did some survey work of our riders," Foster said. "We found that a little over 60% strongly wanted to see us bring more retail experiences into the station environment as part of their commute."
Sound Transit is looking at meeting that demand, where possible.

The next round of vending rollouts aim to put Seattle on the map, targeting the busiest station in the light rail system – Westlake – and the highest performing Eastside station, Bellevue Downtown. Westlake averages about 17,000 daily boardings, while Bellevue Downtown attracts around 2,500.

"Other pilots in the works include mobile coffee carts at Westlake mezzanine," Olson said. "We're also in the final stages of permitting a few beverage carts in the Bellevue Downtown Station. We're also scoping potential locations for vending machines at some stations. Initially, the three Federal Way Extension stations have good potential."

Westlake used to feature direct access to Nordstrom's department store from the mezzanine level, but that door has since been closed, with security cited as the reason. There is still a connection to Westlake Mall.

While the agency has been gradually rolling out pilot projects, staff has also been refining its broader vision for station activation. Foster pointed to hosting the FIFA World Cup and expanding the 2 Line across Lake Washington as watershed moments that pushed the agency to zoom out and look bigger picture about its longer term goals around retail and activation.

Earlier this year, as part of World Cup operations, Sound Transit set up an information booth in the former bus pass kiosk at Westlake, which had been turned into a security booth. Since then, the agency has kept the kiosk open.

"So, this is our strategic vision for station activation: We're striving to make each station reflective of the community in which it sits," Olson said. "Station activation will transform waiting and transitional spaces into engaging, welcoming, and community-centered environments that improve passenger experience."
The visioning work identified four pillars to station activation.

"Sound Transit is organizing station activations within four pillars that activate, engage, partner, and manage," Olson said. "Coffee carts, beverage vendors, farmers markets, food carts, pop-up retail, those will all be defined as 'activate' with an outcome of increased customer satisfaction and passenger comfort."
Sound Transit hosted 22 farmers markets this year at Angle Lake Station, Olson noted, with the help of African Community Housing and Development Ground, which organized the markets.

"Sound Transit is seeking an outcome of stronger emotional connection for passengers with their transit experience," Olson said. "Think live music, local artist features, arts and crafts, cultural celebrations. Sound Transit plans to continue to partner with local businesses and community organizations and artists."

The agency's "partner" pillar simply denotes an intent to increase partnerships with local businesses and community organizations and artists. Manage, meanwhile, was focused on crowd management during high-ridership events.

"The FIFA World Cup was held this summer. Sound Transit worked with over a dozen vendors to create programming at numerous stations downtown and across the system," Olson said. "Memorably, one of the most popular performances was the group that dressed up as astronauts and engage the crowds waiting to board the trains at International District Chinatown stations. These activities help create a festive atmosphere. They help the crowd spirits stay high, even when they were facing the long boarding times – great examples of implementing how we managed as a pillar of activation, integrating activities at stations to help manage the crowds."

Sound Transit has also advanced plans at Sounder stations and is considering Tacoma T Line streetcar stations. On the Sounder S Line, Auburn and Kent have retail as part of transit-oriented development projects. The staff presentation called out the five following early activation projects:

Through the first phase of study, Sound Transit also improved mapping of station areas, with an eye to making it easier to throw events, such as farmers markets or festivals on the premises. For example, staff slides featured a Lynnwood City Center Station map that called areas that would require fire marshal approval to stage for events, while recommending locations for a main stage, tents, portable restrooms, food trucks, and additional food services.

Based on its initial research, Sound Transit appears to be gravitating toward outsourcing the work of overseeing and/or designing the retail program to third-party contractors – which is a well-established pattern for an agency, with outside vendors also performing core functions like security, transit engineering, marketing, etc.

"One of the critical things is what is our management model?" Foster said. "Is this something Sound Transit manages itself like we do our system, or do we bring in industry expertise? In this case, I think we're leaning, based on the experience of our team and talking with other systems across the country, that we should potentially bring in some third-party partners who are experts in retail to help manage this component of our system."

Part of the obstacle to rolling out food service enterprises are health code requirements for bathrooms and sinks and other utilities and infrastructure that many stations lack, at least in the public portion of the station.

"Whether it's utilities or access to restrooms, the very specific requirements of Seattle King County Public Health around that and other public health agencies, that's critical work that we'll be doing as part of that next phase," Foster said, which he said they expected to return in 2027 to share with the board.

While the first two phases of Sound Transit's expansions have been completed with very few retail venues included in stations and limited opportunities to easily add them after the fact, Sound Transit 3 (ST3) projects are still in fairly early phases of design and present opportunities for retail and community spaces to be incorporated from jump. Of course, the catch is that ST3 projects are already under severe budgetary strain and could face pressure to avoid costs seen as tertiary or optional in order to ensure the projects make it across the finish line.

On the other hand, some have argued that rider comfort and basic amenities that improve it should not be treated as expendable and easily jettisoned. Retrofitting those amenities later could end up being more expensive in the long-run with less optimal outcomes possible when not designing stations for activation from the beginning.

King County Councilmember Claudia Balducci said that work to retrofit retail facilities into existing stations could in turn expand rider amenities for non-patrons by providing public bathrooms at more stations. Conversely, designing stations to have public bathrooms from day one is good not just for retail and festival opportunities, but also for the daily rider experience.

"I just want to add my voice to anything we can do to make the station areas more comfortable for our riders," Balducci said. "As we do longer term retail leases, particularly, I'm very supportive of us working with our partners to open those bathrooms to riders that exist for the purposes of whatever retail they may be doing."

articles.title: OPINION | Why Domestic Violence Survivors Fear the Systems Meant to Protect Us
paras: In my experience, as a survivor of domestic violence, victim blaming does not always come from the abuser. It can also come from friends, family, and the big institutions meant to "protect" people, particularly the U.S. criminal justice system.

Growing up, I witnessed and heard stories of South Asian women fleeing violence and attempted "honor killings" by fathers, husbands, brothers, and men they rejected. Many women in my culture don't even tell their family when they've been assaulted or raped by a man, because we know we will be blamed for it. We are taught to fear the consequences of speaking up more than the violence committed against us. And men take advantage of our vulnerability, our silence, our fear, and continue to get away with abusing and exploiting us.

In Washington state, women who defend themselves from abuse can be jailed for their response to violence, while their abusers roam free. The majority of incarcerated women report experiencing trauma, child sexual molestation, domestic violence, intimate partner violence, and other forms of gender-based violence prior to incarceration — this cycle is often called the abuse-to-prison pipeline .
Did you know that about 90% of women who are in prison for killing a man had been previously abused by that same man?

Women are often criminalized more than men for actions taken to protect themselves or their children. Women who kill their male partners receive significantly harsher prison sentences , averaging around 15 years, while men who kill their female partners typically serve only two to five years. Many incarcerated women who fought back against abusive partners did so after years of prolonged abuse, trauma, and living in constant survival mode. When you have spent so long with a dysregulated nervous system, having your basic needs stripped, living in unsafe and abusive environments, your decisions are a trauma response shaped by the need to feel safe, survive, or simply stay alive.

Additionally, incarcerated women are still not safe; they continue to experience sexual harassment, assault, and abuse by male correctional staff and law enforcement officers. Even after surviving abuse, women are subjected to further institutional harm, with no power to seek accountability.

Nonprofits and state-run victim support organizations often prioritize securing grants, covering operational costs, and paying executive staff while treating their case managers as disposable. Meanwhile, most of their funding often comes from the same places that are contributing to gender-based violence and economic exploitation. For example, government agencies that fund victim services also operate within the same criminal legal systems that perpetuate harm, criminalize survivors, and fail to hold abusers accountable.
Gender-based violence is a product of systemic failures, including nonprofit failures.

Most domestic violence programs in Washington primarily serve survivors of intimate partner violence, often overlooking other forms of gender-based violence, including family violence, forced marriage, and workplace harassment. As a previous domestic violence advocate for a community-based nonprofit, I had about 17 cases a month of women who were fleeing violence from husbands and had children, sometimes even living in cars with a newborn baby. And there was no housing. Shelters in King County were always booked and full. My clients had nowhere to go, and we, as case managers, often had to refer them to Pierce County, far from their children's schools, support systems, and communities.

In my role, I witnessed abusers, particularly abusive husbands, call the cops on their wives for fleeing with their child after she had faced years of abuse and violence. I also saw cops arrest survivors who then had to spend nights in jail because the abuser called 911 first or spoke better English than the survivor. Some survivors also had to explain the situations in English without an interpreter, which led their statements to often be misunderstood or for them to be perceived as the aggressor; then they were arrested.
Men protect men. So often, I witnessed male police officers take the side of the men in domestic disputes instead of the women.

Sometimes, my clients were given parking tickets, fines, had their cars impounded, or were criminalized simply for being homeless and living in their cars. CPS was called on mothers living with their children in cars or being in public places for too long. Survivors were also treated as neglectful because they cannot immediately provide stable housing, transportation, or childcare, even when those conditions are connected to the abuse.

I know what it feels like to experience domestic violence and to have the very systems that claim to protect you become another source of fear. I know what it means to choose between protecting yourself and protecting "loved" ones, even when they are the ones causing you harm.

Recently, I saw a post about the Seattle Police Department shooting a woman during a Beacon Hill domestic violence call. My immediate thought was, what would have happened to me if I had chosen to file a police report or if the police had shown up at my home?

For many survivors, fear isn't just of our abusers, but it is also the fear of the systems we are told to trust for protection. Today, we continue our failure to address gender-based violence, in part because we have failed to resolve both its root causes and the systems that allow it to persist: housing instability, poverty, sexism, patriarchal power structures, criminalization and mass incarceration, lack of community support, and inaccessible survivor services.
Until we make these changes, women will remain in harm's way.
If you've experienced gender-based violence, there are places to seek help. You can find more information in the Emerald's " A Seattle Resource Guide for Survivors of Sexual Violence ."

articles.title: Seattle Real Time Crime Center video captures Capitol Hill armed carjacking attempt but suspects elude police
articles.author: Justin Carder
paras: It will be a quieter holiday week on CHS but we’re still working. See something others should know about? Email CHS or call/txt (206) 399-5959 . You can view recent CHS 911 coverage here. Hear sirens and wondering what’s going on? Check out reports from @jseattle or join and check in with neighbors in the CHS Facebook Group .

Surveillance cameras part of Seattle’s Real Time Crime Center captured video of an armed attempted carjacking that ended on Capitol Hill early Saturday morning but the suspects were able to elude officers following a brief I-5 pursuit, according to the Seattle Police Department .

The incident unfolded around 12:22 AM when a frantic driver sped up to officers patrolling the nightlife district near the 1000 block of E Pike. The victim reported that a Dodge SUV carrying four men had been chasing him, and that an occupant of the SUV armed with a firearm exited the vehicle at one point and tried to enter his car before he managed to flee.
Using the city’s camera network, police say the Real Time Crime Center located video evidence showing the victim’s account of the chase and armed confrontation.

Using the suspect vehicle’s description, officers canvassed the area and spotted a matching Dodge SUV leaving the neighborhood. Police attempted a traffic stop before the SUV could merge onto southbound I-5, but the driver refused to pull over.
Officers were authorized to begin pursuit heading south on I-5, though police eventually were forced to terminate the chase near the city limits, SPD said.

SPD said the Tacoma Police Department contacted the Dodge’s registered owner, who claimed the SUV had been stolen without having yet been reported. No arrests have been announced as the investigation continues.

The incident comes as Mayor Katie Wilson has signed off on the expansion of SPD’s Real Time Crime Center camera system that will include new installations on Capitol Hill in the Pike/Pine area and in the Central District around Garfield High School . Officials have vowed to address privacy and law enforcement overreach concerns identified in audits of the system.
Even as the the city moves forward with the new installations, SPD has access to Seattle Department of Transportation cameras in the area around where Saturday’s incident took place.

One audit found Real Time Crime Center staff have access to view 538 cameras under the current system. Private camera integrations through Axon’s “Connect Seattle” program also tie into the system, operating without caps, deployment criteria, or technical masking to prevent private areas such as residential windows from being filmed

articles.title: Wilson, Zahilay make their pick for interim leader to oversee downsizing of King County Regional Homelessness Authority
articles.author: CHS Staff
paras: Seattle Mayor Katie Wilson and King County Executive Girmay Zahilay have tapped Mark Ellerbrook to serve as interim CEO of the King County Regional Homelessness Authority.

The move follows the resignation of Kelly Kinnison earlier this month . Kinnison was hired in 2024 as the troubled organization’s fifth leader and was part of the effort to surface the financial issues that have the authority in a $16.7 million hole.

Wilson and Zahilay’s announcement says Ellerbrook brings nearly 20 years of city and county experience in housing and government administration, most recently serving as as part of Wilson’s leadership team at City Hall. He will take a leave of absence from the city to step into the role.

With approval by the KCRHA Governing Board, the announcement says Ellerbrook’s priorities will include strengthening the agency’s financial controls, navigating uncertain federal Continuum of Care funding, and overseeing the January 1, 2027 transition of locally funded contracts back to Seattle and King County.
The downsizing of the authority began this summer as officials were forced to restructure the KCRHA after the audit was revealed.
The KCHRA’s budget was proposed as $205 million in 2026 with about 60% coming from Seattle and the rest from the county and state and federal pass-through grants.
Some continue to call for the downsizing organization to be shut down completely.

The authority was formed as officials pledged the new effort would consolidate efforts to address the homelessness crisis at a broader, more regional level. At one point growing to a $250 million a year effort, KCRHA was officially established in late 2019 through an Interlocal Agreement between the county and the City of Seattle under then- Mayor Jenny Durkan and then- King County Executive Dow Constantine .

articles.title: Voters are fed up with for-profit utilities, but they keep rejecting ‘public power’
articles.author: Jesse Nichols
paras: Climate activists around the country saw this month’s midterm elections as a win. From congressional seats to governors’ mansions to local offices, progressive candidates leveraged voters’ frustration with the rising cost of living, especially high power bills, to defeat fossil fuel-friendly challengers.

But voters in two communities — Ann Arbor, Michigan, and Kitsap County, Washington — also rejected an idea that some say can address both climate change and affordability: replacing for-profit utilities with publicly owned ones.

On average, public utilities in the country charge lower electric rates and offer more reliable service than for-profit providers. Advocates contend that by being accountable to communities, they could transition to cleaner forms of energy faster than their counterparts beholden to shareholders and bottom lines.

Despite being in different regions of the country, the two community efforts unfolded in eerily similar ways. In each, private utilities spent roughly $2 million on local opposition campaigns, even using identical terms, like “too costly” and “too risky.” In the end, both initiatives failed by single-digit margins, sharing the same fate as the vast majority of recent public power efforts around the country.

These results highlight the unique challenges of creating a new public power utility in the 21st century. A century ago, building a new public utility meant building a new grid. Today, it means buying out the poles and wires already owned by a for-profit utility, a process that more closely resembles a hostile takeover.

Public power has been an important part of Washington’s history for almost as long as Washington has been a state. But the movement really took off in the 1930s, triggered by two major events. First, a citizen-led state ballot initiative gave every community the right to form its own public utility district, or PUD. These new public agencies, run by elected commissioners, were empowered to provide power, water, and eventually internet to their constituents without taking a profit. Soon after, Congress created the Bonneville Power Administration, a New Deal-era agency that sold hydropower from the Columbia River. The new agency was required to give public utilities first dibs on its cheap hydropower, causing dozens of power districts to pop up around the state in the following decades.

It was in this golden age that Kitsap County — a community on the small peninsula across the Puget Sound from Seattle — formed its own public utility district intended to provide electricity. But the outbreak of World War II a few years later delayed that effort for long enough that its authorization expired. Today, the utility district oversees water and internet infrastructure but allows a private utility called Puget Sound Energy to provide power.

By the 1950s, the red-scare movement took aim at public power. Private utility groups ran ads in national magazines. “It was ‘creeping communism,’ and had pictures of Russian dictators,” said Steve Johnson, the former executive director of the Washington Public Utility Association. Since then, public power has been in a dry spell, with most community efforts failing in Washington and across the U.S.

There was a notable exception in 2008, when Jefferson County — Kitsap’s rural neighbor to the west — passed a ballot initiative to create a new public utility that would take over power service from Puget Sound Energy. “I think that was a big wake-up call for the company, because there had not been a new PUD since the 1950s,” said Johnson. Today, Jefferson County runs entirely on carbon-free electricity from Bonneville Power, and typical bills there are roughly 19 percent lower than for Puget Sound Energy’s 1.24 million customers in surrounding areas.

Meanwhile, in neighboring Kitsap County, which today is home to about 280,000 people, Puget Sound Energy’s power rates continued to rise. Over the last five years, the average power bill has nearly doubled, and the company is proposing a series of increases totaling 32 percent by 2029. Puget Sound Energy told Grist that its rates reflect rising demand, infrastructure costs, and the challenge of meeting Washington’s clean electricity targets. State law requires utilities to be carbon neutral by 2030 , leaving Puget Sound Energy, which still gets about half its energy from fossil fuels, scrambling to meet deadlines.

Earlier this year, as bills with new rates arrived in mailboxes, Kitsap utility commissioners started to hear from residents struggling to make ends meet. “Not being able to decide between feeding your kids and paying your electric bill — it’s not OK,” said commissioner Heather Pauley. This led the utility district to put forward a ballot initiative asking voters to give it the authority to take over power service from Puget Sound Energy.

The initiative’s design had, in one commissioner’s words, an “Achilles’ heel.” Voters would be approving the proposal without an official feasibility study. If the measure passed, the district would pay for an extensive study on the plan’s costs and benefits. Only if it penciled out would the commissioners move ahead with taking over the grid. While this was intended as a gesture of fiscal responsibility, it also left voters with few details to vote on.

This ended up being the opening for Puget Sound Energy’s opposition campaign: “Too Costly. Too Risky. No Plan,” their flyers and yard signs read. The campaign spent $2.3 million, making it one of the most expensive local ballot measure fights in state history.

Meanwhile, the public utility district was strictly prohibited from any form of advocacy. “Was there misinformation out there? Absolutely,” said Angela Bennink, the district’s general manager. “But we were limited in what we could do.”

Unplug PSE, a grassroots campaign organized by Johnson and other Kitsap residents, took on the mantle of advocating for the initiative. But with a total budget of $9,000, they were thoroughly outmatched.

Puget Sound Energy also argued that a utility takeover would be too expensive — though much of that expense would come from the private utility itself. During Jefferson County’s buyout negotiations, Puget Sound Energy had demanded $109 million for all its power lines and transformers, more than double their assessed value. The private company was later ordered to return nearly $53 million of those extra proceeds back to its ratepayers. This time, Puget Sound Energy told Grist that it might not even agree to sell in the first place, meaning the public utility would have to pick an eminent domain fight.

With so many voters motivated by affordability concerns, the lack of financial details made the initiative a tough sell. “The ‘No Plan’ of that argument certainly sank in with a lot of people that we talked with,” said Fran Korten, chair of Unplug PSE. In the end, the proposition received only 42 percent approval from voters.

The utility district still has the authority to do a feasibility study, and could potentially make another try for public power in 2028. But Bennink thinks a critical window might be closing. Bonneville Power’s legacy dams and nuclear resources — the resources a theoretical Kitsap County public utility would rely on to provide affordable power to residents — are stretched pretty thin. The administration currently has enough cheap power to cover about 60 percent of the county’s electricity needs, Bennink said, but if another county set up a new public utility, it could claim that power first. This would mean the district could face many of the same market challenges as Puget Sound Energy, the private utility said.

As in much of the rest of the country, public power in Michigan was born out of necessity. For-profit utilities in the late 19th century had little incentive to serve small remote communities, so cities and towns across the Mitten State built their own power systems.
Today, the state has 41 municipally owned electric utilities in small and midsized cities. Almost all of them have been around for decades.

But two years ago, voters in Ann Arbor passed a ballot measure to create a municipal renewable power utility that residents could opt in to. It wouldn’t replace the city’s sole power utility, the for-profit company DTE Energy, but instead would pay for solar panels, batteries, and other infrastructure to feed into the existing grid. As of November, 92 homes in one neighborhood are participating in the pilot phase of the public utility, which aims to expand citywide next year.

But some said this plan didn’t go far enough. The dual-utility model still hinges on DTE’s aging infrastructure, and an analysis by the city indicates that the for-profit utility won’t add renewable energy fast enough to help Ann Arbor reach its 100 percent renewable energy goal by the end of the decade.

So public power advocates in Ann Arbor last year decided to go a step further and push for cutting out DTE, which would allow the city to transition to clean energy faster. They put a proposal on the ballot this year to ask voters whether Ann Arbor should establish a board to lead a transition away from DTE, with the goal of completely replacing the for-profit utility with a brand-new one that’s owned and operated by the city.

“We could make electricity more affordable for people in Ann Arbor. We could make it more reliable,” said Fiona Dunlop, a field organizer for the group Ann Arbor for Public Power, which wrote and advocated for the ballot proposal. “We could take real steps toward good climate policies.”

Supporters of the ballot measure were up against fierce opposition from DTE, labor unions and even the city itself . “The complexity of our proposal made it easier for our opponents to find inroads to attack,” said Brian Geiringer, the executive director of Ann Arbor for Public Power. DTE poured $1.8 million into a group called the Ann Arbor Responsible Energy Coalition, which campaigned against the proposal.

Using the same words as Puget Sound Energy, it argued that movement toward public power would be “too costly and too risky” for Ann Arbor and its roughly 125,000 residents. A board could be made up of people with little to no technical experience and ultimately leave residents with higher costs, the coalition said.

“The people of Ann Arbor saw this proposal for exactly what it was: a mandate that would have made life in Ann Arbor even more expensive by eventually forcing working families to carry the burden of a billion-dollar debt,” the coalition said in a statement after the election, referencing the cost of buying out and maintaining the infrastructure. The $1 billion refers to the coalition’s estimate of how much it would cost the city to buy DTE’s poles and wires, plus how much to maintain that infrastructure. The city estimated in a 2023 early-phase feasibility study that a buyout could cost anywhere from $281 million to $1.15 billion, noting that there’s no modern precedent in Michigan to point to. It could be paid for by issuing bonds, but further financing options would require another feasibility study.
Ultimately, the ballot proposal failed by a slim margin of 3.6 percent, or 2,003 votes.

Like the rest of the country, Ann Arbor residents are frustrated with rising power bills and unreliable service, said Mike Shriberg, a professor of practice and engagement at the University of Michigan’s School for Environment and Sustainability. But the high, uncertain costs of public power might have edged out these concerns, for now. And as in Kitsap County, voters did not have a full feasibility study to consider.
“I don’t think it was actually a debate about the fundamentals of whether public power would be a good thing here in concept,” Shriberg said. “It was really about the details.”

The challenge of creating a new electric utility in the 21st century is “fundamentally different” than it was in the 1930s, Bennink said. A century ago, the power grid was in its infancy, and public utilities were largely building networks from the ground up. Today, creating a public utility instead involves billion-dollar buyouts, well-funded opposition campaigns, and uphill battles with powerful private companies that have every incentive to not cooperate. “It would have been very, very hard,” Bennink said. “Herculean. Monumental.”

Despite the challenges, some say interest in public power will likely keep growing across the country as frustration with utilities continues to mount. “As we’ve seen across the country, there’s an incredible amount of pent-up frustration with our electric utilities,” said Shriberg at the University of Michigan. “Costs are too high, the service is too unreliable and too dirty.”

The lack of details may have been the downfall for the public power ballot questions in Washington and Michigan. But there are signs that government leaders are willing to consider the option if there’s more planning involved. The City Council in Milwaukee, Wisconsin, voted unanimously this month to fund a $1.35 million feasibility study to explore replacing investor-owned We Energies with a city utility. The decision came after the state’s public service commission approved a rate increase for We Energies.

In Kitsap County, many public power supporters are now pushing for a similar plan. At a post-election utility district meeting, the small conference room was unusually packed with residents asking commissioners to perform a feasibility study.

Election Day was “bittersweet” for Ann Arbor organizers going up against utilities. While the public power proposal failed locally, an ambitious statewide ballot measure that would amend Michigan campaign finance laws to rein in utilities’ influence in elections overwhelmingly passed — including among Ann Arbor voters. And public power supporters still see opportunities to move the needle on a grid takeover: The newly elected mayor of Ann Arbor endorsed the public power ballot measure during his campaign, and the City Council saw turnover that could result in a new look at funding for a deeper feasibility study, which failed to pass last year .
“The movement is still very much alive, probably stronger than ever,” Geiringer said.

articles.title: Reclaiming Thanksgiving from a Native perspective
articles.author: Jaelynn Grisso
paras: November is Native American Heritage Month. Thanksgiving Day can be complicated for many Native Americans, including Kristina Pearson, Executive Director of Duwamish Tribal Services.
“Thanksgiving was just something that happened, and you accepted that it happened because this is what people do in America,” she said.

"We're Duwamish, Suquamish, Chinook [and] Snoqualmie,” Pearson said as she introduced herself. “My mother is Cindy. My grandmother is Cecile Hansen. Cecile has been chairwoman for the tribe for 51 years now."
When it comes to Thanksgiving, Pearson thinks about the first winter after Denny party settlers came to the Puget Sound in 1851.

“There were like instances of like folks not being able to feed their babies. And because there weren't necessarily, you know, cows for milk here. And Duwamish people, women,” she paused. “I feel like women don't get enough credit. We talk about Chief Seattle a lot. I have a whole speech where I go into how we're related to Seattle, but then I pivot and I talk about how really, It's about his sister and their mother. So I kind of imagine it to be these the women, right, who would have shown that those colonial women how to use clam juice to feed their babies.”
These days, she says that particular Thursday has become more focused on gathering and being together. As for being grateful? That’s a regular practice

“We went out to harvest some devil's club recently, right, and you leave something as a way to say thank you,” she said. “And that's just an everyday thing. Not on, you know, some obscure day in November.”
A local, grassroots effort allows people living in Seattle, including folks outside of the Native community, to directly support the Duwamish tribe by paying rent.
Jerome Hagen, volunteer for the Duwamish Solidarity Group, explained Real Rent Duwamish .

"It is a way for people to pay a symbolic rent to the tribe,” he said. “Many of us have to pay rent that we have no choice over, but we have the opportunity to pay rent to the first people of this land, the Duwamish tribe, who've been here since time immemorial.”

The rent is symbolic, but the money is real. The program began almost a decade ago to provide material support to the Duwamish people. The Duwamish Tribe is not recognized by the federal government, so it doesn’t get the same powers, funding and services as tribes with recognition.

“The actual origin of Real Rent is there was a conversation that members of the solidarity group were having with Cecile Hansen, the chairwoman of the tribe,” Hagen said. “The thing she said was, if everybody in the Seattle area could just give $1 to the Duwamish tribe, the tribe would be in much better shape. And so out of that conversation, Real Rent was created as a way to make that possible and to create a structure for people to do that.”
For Olivia Johnson from the Duwamish tribe, Real Rent’s impact can’t be understated.

“They helped us to do so much that we've never been able to do before. It's just like night and day. Like, from just being... operated out of, you know, rented offices and business parks all throughout King County to having our own spot, and keeping the legacy of the Duwamish people alive. [That includes] providing services for our tribal members that we were not able to provide before," she said. “We have a lot of tribal members who are very low income, who are struggling, and there are some people in our tribe who really depend on those services to get through the month.”
As Thanksgiving approaches, Hagen says it’s a chance to build relationships.

“We all have an opportunity to have to rethink about Thanksgiving in a way that actually builds towards that true partnership between indigenous people and the other people who have arrived here,” he said. “To be able to use Thanksgiving as a way to build a relationship, to form partnerships with indigenous tribes and indigenous people, to be able to purchase from indigenous tribes, to be able to support indigenous tribes, to help them in their fights and struggles that are going on that can hopefully turn Thanksgiving into something that that we can be proud of as a way to live together in partnership.”
