articles.title: Mpox cases are on the rise again in Brazil – just as an antiviral drug fails in trials
articles.author:
<name>Klinger Soares Faico Filho, Professor de Clínica Médica e Medicina Laboratorial, Universidade Federal de São Paulo (UNIFESP)</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/klinger-soares-faico-filho-2396066"/>
paras: The city of Rio de Janeiro has reported 180 confirmed cases of mpox , an infectious disease caused by the monkeypox virus, MPXV, from Oct. 1 through Nov. 24, 2026.

Skin lesions are the most common sign of the disease. They can also appear in the mouth, on the genitals or in the anal region. Other symptoms include fever, swollen glands, headache, body aches, chills and weakness.

The number of cases in the capital of Rio de Janeiro is more than 22 times higher than the number reported during the same period in 2025. In the state of São Paulo, 128 cases have been identified from Oct.1 through Nov. 17 , which represents almost half of all cases of the disease that the state has reported this year.
The national figures are not alarming: 1,429 confirmed cases and one death as of Nov. 23 , compared to about 10,500 cases and 14 deaths in 2022.

The average, however, hides what really matters: The curve began to rise again in September, concentrated in two state capitals, with a new strain of the virus circulating that is different from the one identified in the previous outbreak.
In virology, a clade is a group of viral lineages that share a common ancestor. Currently, clade Ib predominates among the samples analyzed. The 2022 mpox outbreak was caused by clade IIb.

In response, the Ministry of Health purchased 25,000 doses of the vaccine against the disease and instructed states and municipalities to administer it intradermally – that is, just into the top layer of skin. This technique can increase the number of people vaccinated with the same vial fivefold.
The vaccine has become even more important in the fight against mpox, because the only antiviral drug available to treat the disease has just failed two clinical trials .
Clade Ib was identified in 2023 in the eastern Democratic Republic of Congo and led the World Health Organization to declare an international public health emergency in August 2024.

Following a sustained decline in reported cases in Central and East Africa, the WHO declared the end of this international public health emergency. It was then that prevention, surveillance and control of the disease became part of long-term public health programs.

At the Fiocruz National Institute of Infectious Diseases, or INI/Fiocruz, a leading center for the disease in Rio, 43 of the 62 samples identified between September and October 2026 were from clade Ib. Of the total, only 19 were from clade IIb.

Clade Ib was first detected in Rio in March 2026. The spike in diagnoses did not occur until September. In October, the institute treated 130 people with suspected cases of the disease and confirmed 89 cases.
Clade Ib arrived in Brazil via travelers. INI/Fiocruz identified the first cases with evidence of community transmission – people infected locally, with no recent travel history – in early 2026.

The question is whether clade Ib would cause more severe illness. In Central Africa, it has been associated with a higher case fatality rate than that observed with clade IIb, but this difference is also linked to factors such as malnutrition, co-infections and lack of access to care.

In Rio, INI/Fiocruz has not yet found any clinically significant difference between the two clades in the group of patients being monitored, which they call the Rio cohort. The profile of the most vulnerable individuals remains the same – those with severe immunosuppression, pregnant women and young children. About 45% of the patients in the Rio cohort are living with HIV.

During the 2022 outbreak, the antiviral drug tecovirimat was distributed as a treatment for mpox. The drug had been approved in the U.S. for smallpox based on animal studies, since there was no way to test it on people, as smallpox had been eradicated from the planet since 1980 . But the emergence of mpox has made it possible to approve the drug for people.

An April 2025 trial compared the drug tecovirimat with a placebo in 597 patients with clade I in the Democratic Republic of Congo. The time to lesions clearing up was seven days in the group that received tecovirimat and eight days in the placebo group. This difference is not considered statistically significant.

In February 2026, a second trial settled the question regarding clade II . The study followed more than 400 adults divided into two groups, one that received the antiviral and another that received a placebo. Through Day 29, the estimated rates of lesion resolution were similar in the two groups – 83% with tecovirimat and 84% with the placebo. The study found no evidence that tecovirimat was able to accelerate lesion resolution in adults with clade II mpox.

Thus, mpox remains a disease without a proven specific treatment, which shifts the focus of the response to early diagnosis, isolation and vaccination. The medication remains reserved for patients with severe cases and immunosuppressed patients, even though there is no evidence that it alters the course of the disease in these patients.

The only vaccine for mpox is MVA-BN, also known as Jynneos , a third-generation, nonreplicating smallpox vaccine produced by Bavarian Nordic in Denmark. It has not been tested in randomized trials to assess its efficacy against mpox. There are, however, observational studies conducted in the context of the 2022 outbreak, all involving clade IIb. In these studies, researchers do not determine who receives the vaccine, but simply monitor patient outcomes.

Based on these observational studies, the WHO estimates that this vaccine reduces the risk of mpox by 76% with one dose and by 82% with two , compared to unvaccinated individuals. Results varied from one study to another, particularly with a single dose. Estimates of risk reduction ranged from 35% to 86% with one dose and from 66% to 90% with two doses .
In the U.S., a cohort of at-risk transgender men and women estimated 89% protection with the full vaccination series and 70% with a single dose.

In another study in Germany, the effectiveness of a single dose was 58% overall, but only 35% among people living with HIV – a relevant finding for Brazil, given that nearly half of Brazilian cases occur in patients with HIV. This study also found that in those who have already been exposed, the vaccine reduces the risk of becoming ill by about 20% and appears to lessen the severity of the illness even when it does not prevent infection.

There are two weaknesses in these studies. The first concerns the duration of protection: Antibody levels drop sharply between six and 12 months after the second dose, although the cellular response persists. It is not yet known which of these indicators is a better predictor of protection.

The second is that there is no data on clinical efficacy against clade Ib, though there are laboratory studies. A British group showed in April 2026 that serum from 25 vaccinated healthcare workers neutralizes clade Ib , but at levels consistently lower than those observed against clade IIb. Cross-protection is likely, based on animal models challenged with clade I. The extent of this protection in humans, however, is unknown.

The intradermal injection method, now recommended by Brazil’s Ministry of Health, was adopted in the United States and Europe in 2022 – this method allows the use of one-fifth of the dose – and produced an immune response comparable to that of the subcutaneous method. The costs associated with the vaccine include personnel training and vials of the vaccine that, once thawed, must be used within four weeks.
Right now, prevention is the only way to contain mpox.

The purchase of vaccines for Brazil was made through the Pan American Health Organization Revolving Fund. The initial order of 20,000 doses was increased to 25,000 following negotiations with the manufacturer, with distribution scheduled to begin Nov. 23 .

Prior to that, 3,650 doses from the national stockpile had already been shipped to nine states, including Rio de Janeiro, Ceará and the Federal District. The Unified Health System is limiting vaccination to specific groups: people living with HIV, users of preexposure prophylaxis, or PrEP, laboratory professionals who handle the virus, and medium- or high-risk contacts of confirmed cases. In line with WHO guidelines, there is no mass plan for vaccination. Vaccinations are administered at immunization reference centers rather than primary care clinics.

This decision is based on epidemiological logic and a practical constraint – the global shortage of the vaccine. But the bottleneck in Brazil has not always been supply. Between 2022 and 2023, the country distributed 49,000 doses of the mpox vaccine and administered 14,395 – less than a third.

In a survey of more than 9,500 people of different sexual orientations and gender identities, only 4.9% reported having received at least one dose . The researchers pointed to limited availability and barriers to access as likely explanations for the low coverage.

These same factors are likely to determine whether the 25,000 new doses will make a difference. To protect those at risk before exposure, the vaccine must reach these individuals in time for them to complete the two-dose regimen. This will require that the vaccine be available at facilities that offer PrEP for HIV and at the sexual health clinics these patients already attend – not just at public hospitals where they are unlikely to go.

In the meantime, the Ministry of Health is encouraging anyone who develops new skin lesions – especially if accompanied by a fever or swollen lymph nodes – to seek medical care and avoid close physical contact until they have been evaluated. They are also encouraging people with HIV to keep their antiretroviral therapy up to date, because immunosuppression, rather than the clade, determines who becomes severely ill with mpox.
This is a translation of this article from The Conversation Brazil. This version has been updated to reflect new case numbers at the time of publication.
Klinger Soares Faíco Filho is the founder of InfectoCast, a podcast dedicated to medical education.

articles.title: What are AI chips, and what’s so special about Nvidia’s?
articles.author:
<name>Jeffrey Young, Principal Research Scientist, Partnership for an Advanced Computing Environment, Georgia Institute of Technology</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/jeffrey-young-1631845"/>
paras: The commotion around Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s ouster and reinstatement , the central role of Nvidia in the U.S.-China AI competition , and the U.S. economy’s reliance on the AI boom might leave you asking: What’s so special about Nvidia’s chips?
The answer comes down to graphics processing units, or GPUs, and how far they’ve come from their humble beginnings as sidekicks to computers’ main chips: central processing units, or CPUs.
GPUs now power the most visible advances in generative artificial intelligence, but they began as modestly priced add-on cards for video games and video rendering.

As a researcher of high-performance computing and computer processors, I see three factors that explain how GPUs have become so important to the modern economy and how Nvidia became their dominant supplier: software that made GPUs useful beyond graphics, a research breakthrough that showed what they could do for AI, and a global commercial and political race to build ever-larger AI models.

The CPU is built to handle a wide variety of complicated tasks quickly, a few at a time. In contrast, a GPU typically operates on simpler mathematical tasks, such as multiplying two sets of numbers, but it can perform many of these simpler operations in parallel.

A GPU’s design turns out to be ideal for AI. Training a neural network, the kind of AI model behind today’s chatbots and image generators, comes down mostly to multiplying enormous grids of numbers, over and over. Today’s top AI GPUs can perform more than a quadrillion , or thousand trillion, of these operations every second.

Early GPUs could only draw graphics. Programmers controlled them with small programs called shaders, which calculate things such as the color of each pixel and which can be repeated across millions of pixels in parallel. Nvidia dominated the market for graphics chips in the late 1990s and 2000s.

In the early 2000s, Stanford University researchers built software tools that let programmers use this hardware for other kinds of calculations. That work provided the basis for Nvidia’s Compute Unified Device Architecture, or CUDA, which was released in 2007. CUDA allowed scientists and engineers to run scientific and more general purpose programs using the GPU’s parallel execution model.

The second major shift occurred when AlexNet , a neural network model developed and trained on GPUs, won the 2012 ImageNet challenge, an annual competition to see which software could most accurately identify objects in a set of photographs. AlexNet was trained on two Nvidia GPUs, and it made far fewer mistakes than any competitor. The result showed that GPUs made it practical to train neural networks big enough to beat the older techniques, and AI researchers quickly adopted them for their work.

Because Nvidia had spent years building CUDA and the software around it, it was positioned to benefit more than anyone. Competitors, including AMD, which also makes GPUs, and Google, which designs its own AI chips, called tensor processing units, have since built strong alternatives.

Nvidia and other chipmakers then began redesigning GPUs for AI with specific features. These include adding hardware specialized for the matrix multiplication math that neural networks rely on, using reduced precision numbers to improve the speed of neural network training and adding larger amounts of fast memory to keep these chips supplied with data for AI workloads.

In 2017, Google researchers introduced the transformer , a neural network design originally built to translate between languages. Transformers turned out to perform remarkably well in terms of accuracy as the model and dataset size grew, and this design became the foundation of today’s chatbots and many other generative AI systems.

The growth of these new transformer models has also led to the current boom of generative AI companies, including U.S.-based companies OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta, Google and xAI, as well as Chinese companies such as DeepSeek, Alibaba and Baidu. Each of these companies is actively focused on building large data centers composed of high-end GPUs to train next-generation foundation models.

These foundation models, exemplified by Google’s Gemini, Anthropic’s Claude Fable and OpenAI’s GPT Astra, are very large neural networks that can reason, write software code and analyze information in response to plain language instructions. The companies working on foundation model training are betting that the best models will automate much of the world’s information work and generate enormous economic returns.

Nvidia trains some AI models of its own, but most of its profit comes from selling the chips and software that other companies use to build theirs. This AI boom has led to record profits for Nvidia , but it has also drawn attention from the U.S. government, which has debated how far to restrict sales of advanced chips to China. The Trump administration tightened its export controls for advanced GPUs in the immediate aftermath of the scandal involving Huang’s relationship with an alleged Chinese spy .

Demand for AI chips looks likely to keep growing as the leading AI companies compete to build more capable models, but the boom faces real limits. AI data centers require enormous amounts of electricity , raising questions about the power costs and environmental impacts to local communities.

The most advanced AI chips, including Nvidia’s, are fabricated largely by one company, Taiwanese chip giant Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co., known as TSMC. Demand for AI hardware has also strained supplies of memory chips , creating shortages that reach gaming graphics cards and smartphones.

Nvidia also faces direct competition from AMD, cloud companies designing their own chips, and startups, all promising to run AI more cheaply and with less power. Whether Nvidia’s software and hardware advantages can hold off these challengers is one of the biggest open questions in the industry.
Jeffrey Young has received donations from NVIDIA academic hardware grant programs in the past and has coauthored academic publications with current and former NVIDIA employees.

articles.title: Companies are getting less accurate data on extreme weather just when they need it the most
articles.author:
<name>Suvrat Dhanorkar, Associate Professor of Operations Management, Georgia Institute of Technology</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/suvrat-dhanorkar-579449"/>
paras: The extreme weather fueled by an unusually intense El Niño has caused flooding in low-lying Florida communities, hammered the California coast and upended hurricane patterns – just to name a few examples.

But it also poses a growing challenge for companies that need timely climate data to manage supply chains. This information is disappearing due to federal budget cuts, leaving businesses less prepared to handle the impact of extreme weather.

To be sure, forecasters saw the 2026 El Niño coming. The Climate Prediction Center at the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration, or NOAA, has been forecasting a very strong El Niño since the spring, and its October update put the odds at 83% that this El Niño will become the strongest since record-keeping began in 1950, likely lasting into early 2027.
That kind of warning is valuable. It gives companies months to stock up, reroute shipments and line up backup suppliers before storms arrive or droughts set in.

But bit by bit, other valuable sources of climate data are getting cut. That includes a federal database on disasters, which adds up costs weeks after the event, that NOAA stopped updating in May 2025. The Trump administration has also cut or undercut federal climate analyses, as well as staff and funding for daily forecasting , which has left large parts of the country without coverage during extreme events – a risky prospect for businesses.

As a scholar of business operations and sustainability , I believe these cuts could have cascading effects on companies and supply chains by leaving them more vulnerable to future weather disasters. Eventually, these disruptions will hit consumers as well through higher prices.

In North America, El Niño weather patterns are linked to severe storms in the Pacific, as well as floods, fires and droughts . The economic hit can be substantial, from transportation delays to massive crop failures. Strong El Niño events have historically cost the global economy trillions of dollars .

This El Niño arrives as the pace of natural disasters picks up. While the U.S. averaged fewer than five “billion-dollar” disasters a year in the 1980s, that number now stands above 20 a year – a huge leap, even accounting for inflation. And the 2023 and 2024 totals were the highest on record.

While the scope of weather damage gets worse and worse, critical data is missing. That includes NOAA’s decision to retire its “Billion-Dollar Weather and Climate Disasters” database, ending updates after 2024.

For more than four decades, it tracked the cost of U.S. weather disasters after the fact – and businesses and researchers alike have relied on it to build prediction models. For example, scientists use these historical records to put odds on future losses or to forecast economic activity . Some of my own research also relies on historically accurate climate and weather data.
Unfortunately, the gap in climate science may be widening.

In 2025 the federal government shut down Climate.gov, which served as a central repository for weather and climate data, while its El Niño blog has been frozen since June 2025. The National Climate Assessments, the U.S. government’s preeminent reports on climate science, were taken offline , while the National Weather Service cited staff shortages as it cut back weather balloon launches at multiple sites , which feed forecast models.

Fortunately, some of these data-gathering efforts have migrated elsewhere. The scientists behind the El Niño blog have moved to a nonprofit , while another nonprofit is carrying on the efforts behind the billion-dollar disaster database.

The Trump administration has justified these cuts by citing high administrative costs and potential errors in the prediction models. But that still leaves companies, which lean on public weather data more than most shoppers realize, scrambling.

In many industries, including retail, food processing and agriculture, the payoff from acting early to safeguard supply chains can be large. Real-time and near-real-time data is used in supply chains for enhancing crop yields, finding the best routes for transport, inventory planning, and ensuring worker safety during weather emergencies. For example, Walmart invests heavily in technology and specialists to monitor weather-related disruptions and build resilient supply chains.

Another example is insurance companies, which use weather data for designing commercial insurance policies and processing claims. Risk Management Solutions Inc., a leading catastrophe risk-modeling company owned by Moody’s Corp., regularly use NOAA’s hurricane datasets to inform its advanced risk models.

When public climate data disappears, companies still need timely information to run their supply chains, so some will pay for alternative data. This typically comes from paid private services and subscriptions. Startups such as WindBorne Systems, Sofar Ocean, Tomorrow.io, Black Swift Technologies and Saildrone offer private weather balloon data and advanced climate prediction services.

While privatization can fill some gaps, it’s usually only the large retailers and insurers who can afford these forecasts. Smaller suppliers, local farmers and independent truckers further up the supply chain often can’t.
And that’s exactly where many disruptions begin.

Shoppers feel these disruptions when shortages feed into higher prices, often months later. In 2024, for example, extreme weather in the Americas, including Florida, pushed U.S. orange juice prices to an all-time high that fall. They have have stayed elevated since hurricanes Helene and Milton battered Florida’s groves.
Holiday staples are also not spared. A 2021 heat dome in the Pacific Northwest led to major damage to Christmas tree farms, causing their prices to rise an additional 5% to 10% that year .
And these effects are often global. Poor rains in West Africa more than doubled cocoa prices in 2024, and that inflation is still feeding into U.S. chocolate prices, which were up 14% in 2026 .
A historic El Niño, arriving just as federal climate data becomes sparse, makes this winter an ideal, if unfortunate, test of what climate information is really worth.

articles.title: Prepaid electricity can make bills more predictable, but not necessarily more affordable
articles.author:
<name>Destenie Nock, Alex Hills Career Development Associate Professor of Engineering and Public Policy, Civil and Environmental Engineering, Carnegie Mellon University</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/destenie-nock-2738261"/>
paras: The last house I rented in Massachusetts had an oil heating tank that cost US$800 each time my roommates and I wanted to refill it. If the tank ran out, there was no heat in the home, and we had to pay extra for an emergency refill and for someone to relight the pilot. A full tank of oil could last up to a month and a half – but only if we kept the heat at 55 degrees Fahrenheit (13 degrees Celsius) when we were home and cut it off when we went to work.
Where I live now, in Pennsylvania, we use natural gas and pay afterward, based on our use. It amounts to $200 to $400 monthly – and lets us keep our heat around 70 F (21 C).

Prepaying for heat in Massachusetts certainly made me more aware of how much heating a home cost, but it didn’t make energy cheaper or help me live according to modern standards. Instead, I got used to wearing my winter coat indoors. This is still a concern for many: As winter 2026 approached, some families in Maine that have oil heat had their kids sleep in snowsuits to use less fuel and keep costs down.

Most electricity companies bill for energy already used – like the natural gas company I have in Pennsylvania. But in Maryland, Baltimore Gas and Electric is proposing a prepaid electricity program , similar to my Massachusetts oil setup.

As an energy affordability researcher studying how people change their habits to use less energy when it’s expensive , the real question for me is what this type of payment system would mean for customers. Helping households manage electricity bills is different from ensuring they can afford to use enough energy at home to keep themselves safe.

BGE, which serves approximately 1.3 million electric customers, asked Maryland Public Service Commission members to approve a prepaid program for customers in July 2026. The company says this would help people keep a better handle on their energy spending .

Rather than getting a monthly bill, customers who opted into the plan would make an initial $40 payment toward future electricity use . They could then monitor their power usage and get alerts when balances run low.

The utility’s vice president of regulatory policy and strategy, John Frain, told the Maryland Public Service Commission that prepaid customers wouldn’t have to pay security deposits to open new accounts and wouldn’t have to worry about late payment or reconnection fees if service were disconnected because they weren’t able to pay their bills.

For customers with unpaid balances of up to $1,000, the company would have 25% of each prepayment applied to previous debts and 75% go toward future electricity costs. The company expects to save a yet-undetermined amount of money on collection efforts.
Consumer advocates warn that prepaid billing could cause problems for customers while making life easier for the utility company.
For instance, people on fixed incomes, such as Social Security, could experience increased mental stress because of frequent fears their electricity might be cut off .

They also might make significant changes in their lifestyles: A 2014 study in New Zealand found customers who prepaid for their electricity rationed their own power by, for instance, turning on an electric water heater only every third day and taking cold showers on other days.

Because Maryland prepaid customers would pay the same electricity rates as everyone else, any bill savings would likely come from living without many of the basic services electricity brings to modern life .

The company’s response to this concern is that while customers whose balance gets to zero will be disconnected – as soon as the next day – they’ll have an easier time getting reconnected . Once people add $15 to their account, power can be restored in less than 30 minutes .

But even short disconnections can cause big problems. For people dependent on electric-powered medical devices, such as breathing equipment or home dialysis machines , getting disconnected can injure or kill them. Without the power to charge a phone or power a Wi-Fi router, some people may have trouble getting alerts about their balance or making payments to turn their electricity back on.

Under traditional billing, Maryland law gives customers protections against rapid disconnections. When people are late paying their bills, utilities have to notify them of the overdue balance and give them at least 14 days to pay before cutting off power – a period during which they can still use electricity.
This delay gives people a chance to make payment arrangements and seek financial assistance , such as from the state’s Office of Home Energy Programs .
Applying to that office allows customers to request an additional 55-day reprieve from disconnection , which can help families stay connected during extreme weather events.
In August 2019, BGE conducted a trial run of the prepaid system with 527 customers.

An independent analysis found that power disconnections were often shorter – five hours on average – for prepaid customers than for customers who were billed later for the power they used, whose power was off for an average of 9.4 days. But 10% of prepaid customers had their power cut off at some point during the test period, compared with just 1% of those in the traditional billing program.

The trial run generated some positive outcomes for customers: 61% of the participants said they had better control over their energy bills by being able to decide when and how much to prepay, and 34% said the program’s feature of progressively paying off overdue bills helped them.
However, 41% of participants left before the program formally ended in November 2020. Among those who left , one-third didn’t like making frequent payments, and 23% felt their energy cost more.
BGE told Maryland officials that the prepaid program is “ not intended as a cost-savings program for customers .”
The company says its prepay program offers customers online tools to monitor their energy use and the option to make payments when it’s financially convenient.
But BGE customers can already do both of those things online .

And a utility that cuts people off for running out of credit has less incentive to help customers actually afford sufficient levels of energy to live their lives. That’s because investor-owned utilities generally don’t earn money on selling more electricity, but rather on building and maintaining power lines and substations . In fact, if systemwide energy use drops – due to mild weather or people choosing to use less energy – and the utility collects less than its approved revenue target, then Maryland law lets it charge customers more so the utility can cover its costs and still make a profit .

The Maryland Public Service Commission will decide on BGE’s proposal in January 2027. Its ruling on this prepaid electricity system will determine whether people who seek greater control over their monthly bills would have to give up legal protections that help customers continue to meet their basic energy needs without sacrificing their health and safety during financial hardships .

Destenie Nock is on the board of Clean Energy Works. She has previously received funding from NSF, RK Mellon Foundation, the Sloan Foundation, and the Environmental Protection Agency. She has advocated for disconnection protections for households in regulatory filings and has worked as an expert witness for the AGO in Massachusetts. She is the CEO of Peoples Energy Analytics.

articles.title: California raised minimum wages for fast-food workers – here’s how it played out 2 years later
articles.author:
<name>Liam Sigaud, Research Associate, West Virginia University</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/liam-sigaud-2778708"/>
paras: Even before the 2026 midterm elections delivered a clear message about cost-of-living concerns, many states had been raising their minimum wage on their own as one way to increase workers’ purchasing power. And some have taken a more targeted approach, setting wage floors for specific industries.
As the example of California shows, however, these initiatives can produce mixed results.

In April 2024, California began requiring fast-food chains with at least 60 locations nationwide to pay a minimum wage of US$20 an hour, $4 above the statewide minimum at the time. The governor’s office estimated that more than 500,000 workers would be covered by this mandate.

As a researcher of health and labor markets , I joined with economists David Neumark , Gary Wagner and Vitor Melo to run a study measuring the impact on California’s fast-food industry – specifically, whether restaurants employed fewer workers because of the ensuing higher labor costs.
We found that the answer depends on which establishments you look at.

For the state as a whole, the law didn’t affect employment in any statistically detectable way, we concluded. But smaller chains did take a hit, with employment falling by roughly 20%, while the number of locations dropped by about 10%. New openings fell by 17%-20%, and closures rose by 9%-21%.
This employment decline comes almost entirely from fast-food chains ceasing to operate in California, rather than from staffing cuts at the locations that remain.

The impact of minimum wage hikes holds importance far beyond the fast-food sector. Their proponents point to the fact that the federal minimum wage of $7.25 an hour has stayed unchanged since 2009 and argue that states and municipalities need to take action on their own.

Los Angeles is phasing in a $30 wage for hotel and airport workers, while California’s healthcare workers just received another scheduled increase . Vermont lawmakers have proposed a $20 fast-food wage of their own.
In addition, a total of 16 states will raise their minimum wages across the board on Jan. 1, 2027.
The question of whether and how minimum wages affect employment still provokes a vigorous debate among economists.

In California’s case, some researchers have found that lifting the minimum wage caused small declines in employment compared with other states; others contend that the effect on jobs is essentially zero.
More broadly, some researchers have found that minimum wage hikes cost jobs. But the time horizon matters, and effects tend to get larger in the long run .

Our study didn’t try to settle that disagreement. Instead, we wanted to find out how employers did adjust, and whether large and small chains responded differently. What happens when higher minimum wages raise one sector’s costs and prices while its closest substitutes – such as sit-down restaurants – keep paying the lower statewide minimum wage?

We relied on a database that recorded every business location in the country by name, along with the number of employed workers, each year. That let us directly identify the chains that were subject to California’s law, count each chains’ national footprint to apply the 60-location rule, and track outcomes from 2019 through 2025: total employment, employment at locations that stayed open, the number of locations, and openings and closures.

We also compared California with other states and separately compared each chain’s California restaurants with the same chain’s restaurants elsewhere. Finally, we divided the covered chains into two groups: The 20 largest, which account for about 60% of covered jobs, and the 261 smaller ones.

For the state as a whole, we found that employment at covered restaurants was basically unchanged, and employment at restaurants that stayed open didn’t change. Among the 20 largest chains, there was no detectable effect at all for any of the measures we tracked over this period.
But the smaller chains tell a different story, recording substantial declines in employment, locations and openings, while closures rose.

How to reconcile the flat statewide numbers with the sharp effects on smaller chains? The largest chains employ most of the workers affected by the new minimum wage rule, so the statewide total is dominated by them. And the reduced entry and higher exit among smaller chains may have eased competitive pressure on the largest ones.

A final point: The biggest chains tend to be the most automated, relying more on equipment such as self-serve kiosks that can reduce the number of workers needed. That may help explain the muted employment response among these larger businesses.

First, we caution that the absence of a clear short-run effect on total employment doesn’t prove that the policy won’t cause bigger job losses over time as companies adapt to the new law. We also can’t answer what happened to the workers at the most affected restaurants or what happened to prices at those establishments, although other research suggests they rose by 3% to 4%.

That said, the law was implemented barely 2½ years ago, and some of the larger effects that economists might expect – such as the closure of labor-intensive restaurants or fewer openings – are already apparent among smaller chains.

Second, it’s important to remember that California’s fast-food minimum wage applies only to chains with 60 or more locations. So the smaller chains in that range likely lack the scale, automation and pricing power of the national brands and are most sensitive to the new wage floor. Indeed, the law appears to have shifted California’s fast-food market toward its largest chains, a pattern that other researchers documented in a similar study that looked at Germany’s national minimum wage.

For the cities and states now weighing wage floors of their own, the California evidence isn’t a slam dunk either way. It shows that the costs, broadly speaking, fall first on the smaller chains covered by the law – but whether it meaningfully impacts the largest chains is unclear.
Liam Sigaud is affiliated with the Paragon Health Institute, a not-for-profit health policy research organization.

articles.title: Doctors in Congress used to lean Republican – the 120th Congress marks a historic shift
articles.author:
<name>Michael E. Shepherd, Assistant Professor of Health Management and Policy, University of Michigan</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/michael-e-shepherd-2778177"/>
paras: The 120th Congress, which will be sworn in on Jan. 3, 2027, will have 20 physicians as members, along with twice that number of members who have other professional health backgrounds.

This physician class will make history for including the most Democratic physicians in a single Congress – 11 – in American history – a marked shift from the Republican dominance of previous physician members. These Democratic physicians made their professional expertise and their health policy ideas centerpieces of their campaigns, and now they have the opportunity to advance their health policy agendas.

I am a political scientist who studies the partisan politics of health and health policy in the U.S. While physicians have long shaped American health policy, the physician class elected to the upcoming Congress is the most Democratic in the modern era.

The Democratic physician class in the Senate includes South Carolina’s Annie Andrews, a pediatrician. Andrews made reproductive health and rural healthcare access core tenets of her campaign. For instance, her campaign website stressed that “As a doctor and a mom, I’ve cared for women in some of the most difficult moments of their lives. … I’ll fight to: Restore the protections of Roe v. Wade, Guarantee access to contraception and infertility care, Expand maternal health services, especially in rural areas.”

In the House of Representatives, the Democratic physician class includes California’s Richard Pan, also a pediatrician. Pan’s campaign website , which featured many pictures and references to his physician background and stressed the importance of holding “RFK accountable for endangering Americans” – referring to Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. – as well as fighting to lower prescription drug costs , preventing the continued withering of the Affordable Care Act and banning prior authorization.

Other Democratic medical doctors who will be serving in the 120th Congress include two newly elected members in the House, Adam Hamawy of New Jersey and Amish Shah of Arizona, in addition to six returning representatives. Newly elected to the Senate alongside Andrews is Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan , an epidemiologist with a medical doctorate.

Beyond Congress, Democratic medical doctors will also serve as governors – with Amy Acton newly elected in Ohio and Josh Green reelected in Hawaii – as well as in numerous state legislative positions.

Physicians have played important roles in shaping American politics and health policies, back to the nation’s founding. For instance, Pennsylvania’s Dr. Benjamin Rush , an early public health advocate who led the city of Philadelphia through the yellow fever epidemic of 1793 , was the only person with a medical degree to sign the Declaration of Independence.

Since the late 1980s, the number of physicians serving in Congress has increased substantially term over term. My colleagues and I have documented this rise , as well as how physician members of the House have influenced policy.

We found that physician members of the House were more active and effective in enacting health policy than other members. Physician members were more likely to sponsor health legislation, and their health bills advanced further in the legislative process. This was true for physicians from both parties, both on and off congressional health-related committees.

Since at least 1973, when our data begin, physician House members’ congressional voting behaviors and their health policies have been more conservative than other members on average, even those of their own parties. For example, we found that physician members were more likely to sponsor bills related to curbing abortion access, repealing the ACA and protecting private sector physician autonomy.

However, one of the most striking changes we observed was the shift from the Republican dominance of physician members of Congress to the steadily increasing number of Democratic physicians elected since 2015. That year, there were just two Democratic physicians in Congress, but the 119th Congress – 2025-2027 – has six Democratic physicians. The upcoming Congress will nearly double that amount, with the largest class of Democratic members with medical doctorates in American history.

It will be the first Democratic physician majority since 1995, during the 103rd Congress, when two out of the three physician House members were Democrats. Before 1995, physician members were much rarer, but the majority of them were Republicans. Between 1995 and 2023, 80% of physician members were Republicans.
These partisan changes reflect the broader partisan shifts within the medical community itself.

For most of the 20th century, the majority of physicians – both in Congress and more generally as a group – were Republicans. The American Medical Association was largely a conservative organization .
The party loyalties of today’s physician class mirror the slowly shifting demographics of physicians as a group.
Since the 1970s – and especially since the 1990s – medical school applicants and new physicians have become more diverse in terms of gender, race and ethnicity.

These groups tend to identify as Democrats at higher rates , though medicine as a field continues to be dominated by white men . Additionally, becoming a physician obviously requires getting an undergraduate and a professional degree, but higher educational attainment alone has also become increasingly related to Democratic support.
Beyond these more glacial demographic changes, three Trump-era events have shaped the political mobilization of Democratic physicians.

First, the partisan politics of COVID-19 and especially the politicization of the COVID-19 vaccine , has been associated with decreasing trust in medicine and science from Republican-aligned voters and an increase in physicians’ Democratic support.

Second, the elevation of Kennedy as HHS secretary , whose own vaccine skepticism has long run contrary to medical science and the advice of physicians, further pitted many physicians against the Republican Party .

Finally, the Supreme Court’s decision in Dobbs v. Jackson Women’s Health, which overturned the Constitutional right to abortion , also appears to have politically mobilized many OB-GYNs and other women’s health professionals in response to threats to the care they provide and their professional livelihoods.
All these factors have contributed to a new physician class in Congress that is more Democratic and liberal in their health policy views than previous years.

Ultimately, what this difference means for future public policy remains to be seen. However, if politicians’ campaign priorities portend their legislative activity, there may be a more active push than Congress has ever seen for health reforms related to reproductive healthcare , rural health , prescription drug pricing , bans on prior authorization requirements by health insurers and maybe even Medicare for all .

articles.title: Transit Advocates Push Larsen to Ditch Car-Centric 'BUILD America 250 Act'
articles.author: Ryan Packer
paras: A Washington congressman is finding himself at the heart of one of the first major fights unfolding ahead of January's Democratic takeover in Congress, with billions of dollars in federal transportation funding on the line.

Among the many leadership positions about to change hands in Washington, the next chair of the House's Transportation and Infrastructure committee is very likely to be Rick Larsen. And Larsen, who represents Washington's 2nd Congressional District including Bellingham, Everett, and the San Juan Islands, is facing pressure from advocates to rethink plans to advance a transportation funding package he negotiated with Congressional Republicans earlier this year, known as the "BUILD America 250 Act."

The BUILD Act was rolled out in May, as a replacement for the expiring, Biden-era Investment in Infrastructure and Jobs Act (IIJA). At the time, Larsen touted the bill as investing $580 billion in "job-creating infrastructure," highlighting elements like a boost in federal funding for ferries.

But as the Bipartisan Policy Center noted at the time , the guaranteed funding levels in the bill would represent a decrease in federal support for public transit compared to the IIJA while at the same time boosting spending on highways.

Analysis from the Georgetown Climate Center concluded that full enactment of the BUILD Act would spike carbon emissions annually by 14 to 22 million metric tons, and lead to more than 1,000 additional road deaths due to a pivot away from safety infrastructure.

So the news that Larsen was planning to use the BUILD Act as the template for the next federal transportation package, in the wake of the largest electoral victory for Democrats since the 1970s was met with widespread alarm among those who follow federal transportation policy.

"We are not starting from scratch. We just don’t have the time to start from scratch, the capacity to start from scratch,” Larsen said in an interview with POLITICO earlier this month. "We have a good bill to start with."
Larsen added that committee members would likely insert additional items "that the Democrats would be more supportive of" while they "move some things around underneath the top line."

Larsen has a reputation for being pro-transit, regularly appearing at Sound Transit ribbon cuttings and referencing his past efforts to secure $1.8 billion in federal funding for Lynnwood Link in 2018. But with transportation funding not likely to get a significant amount of national attention compared to other issues tackled by a newly Democratic Congress, there are no assurances that the flaws in the BUILD America 250 Act are going to be fixed.
Transportation advocacy organizations have been pushing Larsen to fully ditch the BUILD Act, framing the recycling of the bill as a generational mistake.

"Incoming House leaders should not advance a bill that was produced with the help of so many members of Congress who just got sent home by their voters. And on the flip side, the huge influx of new members who were just sent to Washington should get their chance to craft a different approach to transportation—a new Congress should mean a new sheet of paper," Transportation for America's Steve Davis wrote in a blog post on November 6. "The dynamics have certainly changed. A better deal can be had. Congress should bury the BUILD Act and start over fresh."
An action alert to push Larsen has already generated more than 16,000 letters on the issue.

"The BUILD America 250 Act would commit the country to another five years of traffic, pollution, and expensive car dependence while leaving public transit systems without the funding they desperately need," that action alert from National Campaign for Justice noted.

The IIJA expired on September 30, with Congress approving a stopgap spending bill that slashed transit and rail spending that extended that deadline to December 11. Another extension is all but certain,

While future levels of transit spending remain an open question, Larsen will also be tasked with managing the fact that the Trump administration has been refusing to spend the transit funding that's already been approved. In a letter sent earlier this month to Office of Management and Budget Director Russell Vought and the Acting Director of the Federal Transit Administration (FTA), Larsen joined with Senators Patty Murray and Elizabeth Warren to call out "holding infrastructure dollars hostage," per a press release .
Murray is set to take the gavel in the powerful Senate Appropriations committee, putting her in the driver's seat on future federal transportation spending as well.

"[W]e have watched for months as FTA and OMB have stonewalled the progress of worthy transit projects," the letter stated. "Your agencies have neglected for a year to advance the Boston Green Line Transformation project and the Los Angeles Southeast Gateway Line to the [Capital Investment Grant] Engineering phase under current program rules that were adopted in November of 2025 – without any justification or explanation for the delay."

While no Seattle-area transit projects were referenced in the letter, Sound Transit is counting on FTA dollars as it moves toward construction on the West Seattle and Tacoma Dome Link Extension projects, with a failure to secure those grants likely having cascading impacts on a financially strained system expansion plan that already took a big hit earlier this year . Meanwhile, the Draft Environmental Impact Statement (DEIS) for the Ballard Link Extension has been held up by federal review for over a year, only now being released on December 11.

For its part, King County Metro announced this summer it was no longer seeking federal funding for its RapidRide R Line enhanced bus project, preferring to go it alone. Officials framed defederalizing funding as speeding up project delivery given the run around the FTA has given many transit projects. Metro is still counting on federal funding for its RapidRide K Line , which will run between Kirkland's Totem Lake and Eastgate in Bellevue.

The federal threats to transit funding don't stop there. Earlier this fall, FTA advanced a rule change that would revamp eligibility criteria on one of its biggest transit grant programs, making it harder for projects to qualify – and apply retroactively to projects already in the pipeline. If implemented, that would scale back federal transit funding even further, shifting costs back onto transit agencies that aren't prepared to shoulder the burden.

“The new guidance is a part of the Trump administration’s systematic campaign to reduce or eliminate funding for new transit projects,” Yonah Freemark, principal research associate at the Urban Institute, told Streetsblog . “It’s basically a crisis for transit agencies.”

Washington's congressional delegation, including Larsen and Murray, is set to be put in a prime position to be able to help confront that crisis, but it remains to be seen whether that's going to be enough to resist a full-out federal assault on sustainable transportation options including public transit.

articles.title: Harry’s Fine Foods: 10 years of community on Bellevue Ave E — and the roots of its food+drink family’s next leap inside a $4.9M+ Capitol Hill mansion
articles.author: Anne Jorgenson
paras: Renovations underway before Harry’s 2016 debut (Image: Harry’s Fine Foods)
Ten years ago, Julian Hagood was simultaneously working and running his own catering business out of his shared apartment in Capitol Hill. As orders grew, so did the need for a home for the business.

“Knowing that I’ve wanted to be a chef since I was 10 years old, it was always kind of my dream to have my own space and give people my idea of hospitality,” said Hagood. As a neighborhood resident Hagood was familiar with the area, and when the space availed itself, he jumped on the opportunity.
“Seeing the vision for it and what it could possibly be was an exciting thing,” reminisced Hagood.

Named after the corner store that once occupied the space, Harry’s Fine Foods has always strived to be a local watering hole. Their ten-year anniversary celebrates both the accomplishment of a decade and the community that has made the independent restaurant run by a husband and husband team successful.
Surviving, if not always thriving, the restaurant has weathered the peak of the COVID-19 pandemic and rising operational costs, a feat not lost on Hagood and Jake Santelli .
“As the brand recognition of Harry’s has grown, Fine Foods has grown beyond being just a neighborhood restaurant, but I don’t think it’s ever lost its connection to the neighborhood,” said Santelli.

All under the umbrella of the Harry’s Good Times hospitality family, the business has now expanded to four establishments: Harry’s Fine Foods and Harry’s Guest House on Bellevue Ave, Harry’s Beach House on Alki, and upcoming The Baillie on 14th Ave E near Volunteer Park –their most ambitious project yet.
Plans for The Baillie are taking shape at 14th and Aloha

Set to open in late 2027, The Baillie will be a boutique hotel and restaurant on Millionaire’s Row , inside a renovated 113-year-old mansion. Hagood and Santelli plan to make the Baillie a place for both visitors and the neighborhood.
Part hotel, part restaurant, part lounge, The Baillie will maintain space for first, come first served neighborhood patrons.

“We’ve lost spontaneity in the dining experience. The thing that is the proper defining feature of a neighborhood restaurant is that no matter what you don’t need a reservation, you’re going to show up and we’re going to make sure we feed you,” said Santelli.

The couple purchased the historic 11,000-square-foot bed-and-breakfast in February for $4.9 million, and plan to operate seven days a week once opened, welcoming visitors to the neighborhood, be they tourists, passersby, or parents who managed to find a babysitter and want to enjoy a night out.
“We’re all so busy in our lives and work, we’re designing the space in a way that you can make a night of it with the Baillie,” said Santelli.

Taking on the project is a major financial undertaking but the dollars will be nearly eclipsed by the paperwork and navigating the city’s zoning and business laws. Challenges like sorting out hours in this residential area of Capitol Hill will be part of what makes The Baillie special — just like the original Harry’s.
That hospitality mindset is the ethos of Harry’s Good Times, and all of that started with Harry’s Fine Foods in the fall of 2016 .

“What we try and do is just give people a reason to come and see us again. Ideally that will help us – be the best restaurant, be the best operator, be the kindest,” said Santelli. “That’s why we call it Harry’s Good Times — you cannot forget to find joy even when things are going crazy. It’s the best way to get through your life.”

None of this is to say everything has been sunshine and roses, but the couple says they operate with a glass half full mindset. As business costs increase citywide, Hagood and Santelli know that the team and the customers behind Harry’s Fine Foods is what keeps the dream alive.
“We’re not going anywhere, we will always be rooted in that neighborhood mentality.”
That mindset is important to the city right now, especially for independent businesses.

A 2026 Business Climate Survey by the Seattle Metro Chamber and Downtown Seattle Association shows that a majority of restaurants believe that the city’s business climate has worsened over the last year and are pessimistic about the next 12 months.
Along with thanks to the community for the last ten years, Hagood’s parting words were a call to action.
“Go visit your neighborhood restaurants because if you don’t they may not be around much longer — not just Harry’s.”
Harry’s Fine Foods is located at 601 Bellevue Ave E. Learn more at harrysfinefoods.com .

articles.title: Mayor Wilson celebrates ‘Our New Progressive Majority,’ incoming council member in anniversary address
articles.author: Justin Carder
paras: Marking the one-year anniversary of her election win , Seattle Mayor Katie Wilson released a video address celebrating a growing progressive coalition at Seattle City Hall and across the nation, spotlighting the arrival of incoming District 5 Councilmember Nilu Jenks as a pivotal boost for her administration’s agenda.

In her “ Our New Progressive Majority ” address, Wilson framed recent election wins across the nation and in Seattle as a mandate from residents frustrated by homelessness and the rising cost of living. Locally, the centerpiece of that shift is Jenks, the newly elected D5 representative Wilson described as “a pragmatic progressive with whom I’m so excited to work on the Seattle City Council.”

Jenks, who defeated opponent Julie Kang in the November election to represent North Seattle’s District 5, adds a key ally for Wilson’s push on affordable housing, pedestrian safety, and expanded transit. Wilson noted that voters nationwide echoed Seattle’s demand for leadership that will “deliver policies and programs that materially improve people’s lives”.

With Jenks joining the council, Wilson said she will aim to build on her administration’s first-year legislative record, which includes banning rental “junk fees,” fast-tracking shelter expansion, guaranteeing free school meals, and passing a major public transit funding measure. However, the mayor cautioned that governing requires balancing bold progressive ideals with pragmatic execution, pointing to her recent veto of an RV permitting system and her decision to move forward with police CCTV cameras following a privacy audit.

“The big bold progressive initiatives that make headlines need to pass this test, and so does the mundane work of city government — making sure the lights stay on and the potholes get filled,” Wilson said as she urged the new wave of progressive officials to focus on tangible daily results.

articles.title: Best Side Cycling Tests Out New Henderson Bike Lane in Rainier Beach
articles.author: Doug Trumm
paras: Hanoch of the Youtube channel Best Side Cycling visited an important new protected bike facility in Southeast Seattle, which upgraded safety conditions on the crash-prone corridor of S Henderson Street. The new facility safely connects Be'er Sheva Park and Rainier Beach School in the east to the Chief Sealth Trail farther west, linking destinations like South Shore K-8 school and Rainier Beach Pool and Community Center along the way.

The Seattle Department of Transportation (SDOT) incorporated Toronto-style concrete barriers on much of the facility to make sure the bike lane is truly protected. Road medians and speed cushions also provide traffic calming on the speeding-prone thoroughfare, aiding all people using the street. With trees still in their fall glory, it's a great time to ride the facility. That said, Hanoch gave the sage advice to tread carefully over piles of leaves as they can be very slippery, especially when wet.

South Seattle has generally trailed North Seattle and the downtown core in getting high-quality protected bike lanes, and that has contributed to it seeing far more fatal crashes and serious traffic injuries than other districts of the city. SDOT reported 71 crashes in the Henderson segment alone from 2021 to 2022, as Best Side Cycling noted, underscoring the need for the project.

However, bit by bit , SDOT is pushing to make up the gap, with the safe streets community long pressing for a more equitable distribution of safe facilities across the city – flagging that South Seattle was getting left behind. Though delayed, major bike network upgrades are planned in South Beacon Hill (extending the recently completed North Beacon Hill bike lane ) and Georgetown .

As for the new Henderson facility, Hanoch's review was positive: "I don't mean to just glaze SDOT, but this one I really do feel they're taking a lot of the best practices they've seen in a lot of different places, and we will use them here, like this daylighting in front of those that parking. It's much bigger than some other places like on Union Street."

articles.title: Sound Transit Funds Study to Speed Up D Line Bus
articles.author: Doug Trumm
paras: On Thursday, the Sound Transit Board allocated $500,000 to fund a study of bus speed and reliability improvements for the RapidRide D Line, which runs from Downtown Seattle to Ballard and Crown Hill. It's an early signal that D Line riders can expect a faster ride – a few years down the road, anyway.

King County Executive Girmay Zahilay brought forward the budget amendment, with support from Tukwila Mayor Thomas McLeod and the entire Seattle delegation on the agency board: Mayor Katie Wilson, City Councilmember Dan Strauss, and County Councilmember Teresa Mosqueda.

A timeline for the project was not immediately clear, but supporters noted it was important to provide interim improvements while Ballard and Interbay wait on its delayed light rail project. In 2016, the campaign for the successful Sound Transit 3 (ST3) ballot measure pledged to deliver Ballard Link by 2035, but the timeline has slipped since then.

“I’m very, very happy to be sponsoring this amendment, bringing half a million dollars forward, so that Sound Transit and the City and King County can together work to advance the planning and improve the RapidRide D to Ballard," Wilson said. "We know that that’s no substitute for light rail, but right now it is the third busiest route in King County. It carries more than 10,000 riders a day, and making this bus work better will ease the mobility burden in this regional growth center and keep people moving while we do that longer term work.”

Zahilay credited the Save Ballard Rail coalition with raising the need for D Line improvements. Designing the project will entail a collaboration between Sound Transit, the Seattle Department of Transportation (SDOT), and King County Metro. While Metro operates the bus, SDOT maintains the roadway over which it runs, and the Seattle Transit Measure also funds extra service that boosts bus frequency.

"I want to specifically thank Save Ballard Rail, who has been regularly in touch with my staff and asked us to look into ways to expedite improvements to the RapidRide D line," Zahilay said. "This amendment would move $500,000 of already committed funding for this project up to 2027 to ensure that Sound Transit, SDOT, and Metro explore options and start planning for these capital improvements that would be intended to speed up the RapidRide D."

Zahilay reminded the board that ST3 included funding for Seattle bus improvements as an early deliverable . Namely, it included $35 million to "design and implement transit priority improvements along King County Metro’s RapidRide C and D lines that provide service to Ballard and West Seattle as an early deliverable to provide improved speed and reliability, in advance of light rail starting operations to these areas."

"When voters approved Sound Transit 3, they approved a modest amount of funding to advance the RapidRide D resources for capital improvements, bus and traffic signal priority, just to help move people in the interim while the light rail station and light rail was getting to Ballard," Zahilay said.

That funding was a victim of the 2021 realignment vote , which delayed a number of projects due to pandemic-related planning delays and budgetary strain. The early deliverable went from an early deliverable to a late deliverable without a definite timeline.

"This was originally designed to be an early deliverable in 2025, but in 2021, the board voted to delay the timeline as part of a realignment plan, and I want to speed things back up again," Zahilay said. "I think this board has made it clear that getting to Market Street in the long term, as the CEO mentioned, is a priority for this board. And we have also said that, in the short term, we want to improve transit service in that area through transit mitigation efforts."

As it stands, Sound Transit's best-case scenario for light rail to reach Ballard is 2042 – although the agency has granted that many hurdles remain and has not ruled out the opening date slipping to the 2060s if those hurdles are not navigated.
Jonatan Gonzalez, an organizer with Save Ballard Rail, spoke in favor of the amendment at Thursday's board meeting.
"As we know, Ballard is waiting for light rail, and we can improve bus service now," Gonzalez said. "That'd be amazing."
Metro spokesperson Jeff Switzer told The Urbanist that Metro, in partnership with SDOT and Sound Transit, had some earlier planning to build upon, but that those concepts would need updating.

"Following voter approval of this investment in 2016, work began to identify projects that would improve speed and reliability along the corridor," Switzer said. "That effort was paused following the initial realignment process, and Metro plans to update the analysis to identify RapidRide D enhancements that can be delivered in the near term for the benefit of riders."

Wilson and Zahilay both emphasized bus improvements in their successful runs in 2025. Zahilay reiterated that accelerating the R Line project , replacing Route 7 in the Rainier Valley, was a priority for his administration, and recently cleared a King County Council committee approval vote .

One of Wilson's signature moves in her first year, meanwhile, was rapidly rolling out a bus lane for Route 8. Long notorious for its lateness, Route 8 has since seen a dramatic jump in speed and reliability thanks to the street redesign, a project her predecessor, Bruce Harrell, had sought to frame as completely infeasible.

The same style treatment for the D Line could result in huge time savings for riders. The route lacks consistent bus lanes outside of downtown, with SDOT offering brief sections a few blocks at a time rather than a connected treatment.

Another big move for Wilson was a renewal proposal that doubled the size of the Seattle Transit Measure, which will provide funding to boost frequencies on about a dozen bus lines , with the D a likely candidate. The transit measure passed resoundingly in November with more than 72% of the vote.

With the D Line study just now getting off the ground, the scope of the project is not yet clear. Strauss floated the idea of an express bus with reduced stops shadowing the route. He also underscored how slow the bus is now.

"I will state: that RapidRide is very slow," Strauss said. "It is a milk-run bus out to Ballard going through Uptown. Its travel times are 40 to 45 minutes from where you sit right now just to downtown Ballard."
As riders reacted to the news, some disputed the trip times Strauss has quoted as exagerrated.

"Why does he feel the need to pad everything? It's 27 to 36 minutes from Pioneer Square to Market Street depending on time of day," Seattle Transit Blog contributor David Lawson wrote in a Bluesky post . "Lots of room for improvement, but the work that's already been done has made a difference."

One joked that Strauss did not know what a milk run is, alluding to the D's straight rather than circuitous routing. On the other hand, another D Line rider noted reliability and bus bunching issues can add wait times at stops.

Strauss has mentioned on multiple occasions that he thinks the routing through Uptown to serve Seattle Center slows the route down too much. The drawback would be that skipping the Seattle Center would decrease Northwest Seattle's access to that popular destination, and it may require shifting another route over to provide adequate coverage for Uptown.
One way or the other, improvements appear inbound, although just how dramatic and imminent is yet to be determined.

"The RapidRide D Line serves 10,500 riders on an average weekday and is the third busiest route in the region. It provides critical connections between Ballard, Interbay, Uptown, and Downtown Seattle, while also linking customers to other frequent transit services throughout the city," Switzer said. "We look forward to partnering with Sound Transit and SDOT to advance improvements that enhance reliability, speed, and the overall customer experience on this important corridor."

articles.author: Michael Smith
paras: To celebrate 30 years since voters passed Sound Move , Sound Transit is hosting a transit Bingo game today. Sound Move was the Central Puget Sound Regional Transit Authority’s first voter approved funding package to build a regional transit system. The Sound Transit brand was not adopted until 1997. Sound Move included commuter rail between Everett-Seattle and Lakewood-Seattle, light rail in Tacoma and between Seattle-SeaTac, and an extensive network of express buses in Snohomish, King, and Pierce counties.

The first component of Sound Move to enter service, ST Express, began on September 19, 1999 with nine routes. Commuter rail service started the following year with trips between Seattle and Tacoma. The agency’s first light rail line, then-called Tacoma Link, opened in August 2003. Light rail service in Seattle, Central Link, began service on July 18, 2009 between downtown Seattle and Tukwila.

Everyone is invited to explore the region while visiting stations to fill in their Bingo card today between 10am to 2pm.
